title: Other networks worth knowing
lead: Autoencoders and VAEs, GANs, diffusion models, graph networks, physics-informed networks and neural operators, contrastive learning and mixture of experts: what each one optimises, its equations derived, a worked example in numbers, a lab that runs on a laptop, and how each one fails.
prerequisites: Module 01: maximum likelihood and cross-entropy, train/test splits, baselines and leakage, PCA
Module 02: MLPs, backpropagation and reverse-mode autodiff, Adam, writing a PyTorch training loop
Module 03: convolution and weight sharing (the GCN analogy); the U-Net by name
Module 04: attention as a softmax-weighted average (Bahdanau); anomaly detection from forecasting residuals
Probability: Gaussian densities, expectations, conditional distributions, Jensen's inequality
Calculus and linear algebra: the chain rule, eigenvalues and eigenvectors of symmetric matrices, second-order linear ODEs (the damped oscillator)
outcomes: Derive the ELBO in two ways, compute the closed-form Gaussian KL, and detect posterior collapse from KL per dimension and active units.
Build an autoencoder anomaly detector, set its threshold from held-out normal data, and report its false-alarm and detection rates against a PCA baseline.
Derive the optimal GAN discriminator and the Jensen-Shannon objective, explain the non-saturating loss and mode collapse, and state why diffusion displaced GANs for most image work.

Derive the closed-form forward process of a diffusion model, explain the noise-prediction loss through the ELBO and through the score, and train and sample a 2D diffusion model with classifier-free guidance.
Compute a GCN layer by hand from the normalised adjacency, implement message passing from an edge list, and explain over-smoothing from the eigenvalues of the propagation matrix.
Write the loss of a physics-informed network for an ODE or PDE, diagnose the trivial-solution failure, fix it by non-dimensionalising, weighting or hard constraints, and solve an inverse problem.
Describe DeepONet and the Fourier neural operator and state the checks a surrogate needs before it is used on a new design.
Derive InfoNCE as a classification loss with its log N bound, and measure with a linear probe what contrastive pretraining buys when labels are few and how the augmentations decide what is learned.
Count the total and active parameters of a mixture-of-experts model and explain routing collapse and the load-balancing loss.
Choose among these families for an engineering problem and name the baseline each choice must beat.
software: PyTorch 2.x (the CPU build is enough; Google Colab is the free option if you want a GPU, which no lab needs)
scikit-learn (load_digits, make_moons, PCA, LogisticRegression, KNeighborsClassifier, NearestNeighbors, roc_auc_score)

sections.title: A map of the families, and the tools they share
sections.purpose: Orient the reader with a map of what each family solves and optimises, and collect the four mathematical tools the rest of the module uses: KL divergence, Jensen's inequality, Gaussian algebra and Monte Carlo gradients.
must_cover: A map table, one row per family, columns 'problem it solves', 'what it optimises', 'what it outputs': autoencoder (reconstruct x through a bottleneck; squared error); VAE (maximise the ELBO, a lower bound on log p(x)); GAN (a minimax game between generator and discriminator); diffusion (regress the noise added at a random noise level); GNN (a supervised loss on node or graph labels, computed with message-passing layers); PINN (residual of a known differential equation plus data and boundary terms); contrastive learning (InfoNCE: pick the positive among N candidates); mixture of experts (any loss; an architecture that routes each input to k of E experts).

Three ways to build a generator and how they compare: an explicit latent-variable model trained on a likelihood bound (VAE), an implicit model trained adversarially (GAN), a model that learns to undo gradual noising (diffusion). Compare on network evaluations per sample (1, 1, tens to hundreds), training stability, mode coverage, and whether a likelihood or bound is available (bound, none, bound).
KL divergence D_KL(q||p) = E_q[log q/p]. Non-negativity derived from Jensen's inequality: -D_KL = E_q[log p/q] <= log E_q[p/q] = log 1 = 0, with equality iff q = p. Asymmetric, so not a distance.

Closed-form KL between univariate Gaussians: D_KL(N(mu1, s1^2) || N(mu2, s2^2)) = log(s2/s1) + (s1^2 + (mu1 - mu2)^2)/(2 s2^2) - 1/2, derived in three lines (expectation of the difference of two log-densities); special case against N(0, 1): (1/2)(mu^2 + s^2 - log s^2 - 1), used in Section 3.

Gaussian algebra used in Section 5: if a ~ N(0, sa^2) and b ~ N(0, sb^2) are independent then a + b ~ N(0, sa^2 + sb^2); c * N(0, 1) = N(0, c^2); any Gaussian sample can be written mu + sigma * eps with eps ~ N(0, 1).

Monte Carlo: E_p[f(x)] is estimated by an average over samples; the gradient problem when the sampling distribution depends on the parameters, grad_phi E_{q_phi}[f(z)] is not E_{q_phi}[grad_phi f(z)]; stated here, solved in Section 3.
One-sentence reminders with links, not re-derivations: maximum likelihood and cross-entropy (Module 01), reverse-mode autodiff (Module 02), PCA (Module 01).
worked_examples: Forward and reverse KL with q = N(0, 1) and p = N(1, 0.5) (variance 0.5): D_KL(q||p) = log(sqrt(0.5)/1) + (1 + 1)/(2 * 0.5) - 1/2 = -0.3466 + 2 - 0.5 = 1.1534 nats; D_KL(p||q) = log(1/sqrt(0.5)) + (0.5 + 1)/2 - 1/2 = 0.3466 + 0.75 - 0.5 = 0.5966 nats. Different numbers, so KL is not symmetric. Both numbers reappear in Section 3 as the ELBO gap and the KL term of one exact example.

Two noising steps make one: scale x0 = 2 by sqrt(0.8) and add sqrt(0.2) * eps: x1 = 1.7889 + 0.4472 eps ~ N(1.7889, 0.2); with eps1 = 0.5, x1 = 2.0125. A second identical step gives x2 ~ N(1.6, 0.36) given x0, that is sqrt(0.64) x0 + sqrt(0.36) eps with one draw: the variances add and the signal factors multiply. Section 5's closed form is this composition for any number of steps (its own worked example uses x0 = 2, alpha-bar = 0.5, eps = -0.4).

figures.description: Map of the module in two rows. Top row, three generator pipelines: VAE (x -> encoder -> (mu, sigma) -> z -> decoder -> x-hat, labelled 'maximise ELBO'); GAN (z -> G -> fake x -> D <- real x, labelled 'minimax'); diffusion (x0 -> add noise -> ... -> x_T ~ N(0, I), with dashed arrows back labelled 'learned denoiser eps_theta, tens to hundreds of steps'). Bottom row, four boxes: GNN (small graph with arrows converging on one node, 'message passing'), PINN (network u_theta(x, t) feeding a box 'N[u] = 0', 'residual loss'), contrastive (one input -> two augmented views -> encoder -> two points pulled together on a circle, other points pushed apart, 'InfoNCE'), MoE (input -> router -> 2 of 8 expert boxes highlighted, 'top-k'). Each box carries its objective in one line.

checks: Why is D_KL(q||p) never negative? -> Jensen: E_q[log(p/q)] <= log E_q[p/q] = log of the integral of p = log 1 = 0.
Which generator family needs many network evaluations per sample, and why? -> Diffusion: it reverses the noising one step at a time, one network evaluation per step.

sections.title: Autoencoders: bottlenecks, denoising and anomaly detection
sections.purpose: Show what an autoencoder learns, prove that the linear one recovers the PCA subspace, and use reconstruction error as an anomaly score with an honestly chosen threshold.
must_cover: Definition: encoder z = f_phi(x) in R^{d_z}, decoder x-hat = g_theta(z), loss L = (1/N) sum_i ||x_i - g_theta(f_phi(x_i))||^2. Undercomplete (d_z < d_x) means a bottleneck; an overcomplete autoencoder with no other constraint can learn the identity and is useless.

Linear autoencoder = PCA subspace: with centred data, linear f and g and squared error, the optimal product g(f(x)) is the orthogonal projection onto the top d_z eigenvectors of the covariance (Eckart-Young). The autoencoder recovers the subspace, not the individual components, because any invertible d_z x d_z mixing in the code gives the same reconstruction. The mean squared reconstruction error equals the sum of the discarded eigenvalues (Baldi and Hornik 1989).
Nonlinear autoencoders find curved manifolds. Lab 1 numbers on 8x8 digits: at d_z = 2 the autoencoder's test error is 0.037 per pixel against PCA's 0.053; at d_z = 8, 0.011 against 0.025.

Denoising autoencoder: train on a corrupted input (x + noise, or x with pixels masked), target the clean x; the network learns to move points back toward the data. Vincent (2011): for small Gaussian noise of variance sigma^2 the optimal denoiser r satisfies r(x~) - x~ approx sigma^2 * grad log p(x~), a pointer to the score in Section 5.

Anomaly detection: train on normal operation only; score = reconstruction error; set the threshold at a high percentile of the errors on held-out normal data, which fixes the false-alarm rate by construction; the detection rate can only be measured on known anomalies. Classical baseline from process monitoring: PCA's squared prediction error (the Q statistic). Module 04 does the same with forecasting residuals.

How it fails: anomalies that resemble normal data reconstruct well; a change of operating condition shifts normal errors above the threshold; anomalies hidden in the 'normal' training data are learned as normal.
worked_examples: Linear autoencoder by hand: four centred points (2, 2), (-2, -2), (1, -1), (-1, 1). Covariance (1/N) sum x x^T = [[2.5, 1.5], [1.5, 2.5]], eigenvalues 4 and 1 with eigenvectors (1, 1)/sqrt(2) and (1, -1)/sqrt(2). The best one-dimensional code projects onto (1, 1)/sqrt(2): (2, 2) and (-2, -2) reconstruct exactly, (1, -1) and (-1, 1) reconstruct to (0, 0) with squared error 2 each. Mean squared error 4/4 = 1.0, the discarded eigenvalue.

Anomaly threshold with Lab 1's numbers: an autoencoder (d_z = 8) trained on digits 0-8; the 95th percentile of validation errors is 0.0261 per pixel. On the test set 4.0% of normal digits exceed it and 58.3% of the 9s do; ROC AUC 0.952. A PCA (8 components) Q-statistic detector gives AUC 0.791 and detects 22.2% at a 7.7% false-alarm rate. Both numbers matter: an AUC of 0.95 can hide a detection rate too low to be useful at the operating threshold.

figures.description: Autoencoder architecture: an 8x8 digit (64 pixels) -> encoder (64 -> 128 -> d_z) -> bottleneck z drawn as two neurons (d_z = 2) -> decoder (d_z -> 128 -> 64) -> reconstructed digit; a loss arrow compares input and output.

Two panels. Left: the four-point linear-autoencoder example in the plane with the principal axis (1, 1)/sqrt(2), dashed projection lines and hollow circles for reconstructions. Right: Lab 1 histograms of per-pixel reconstruction error for normal test digits (0-8) and for 9s, the threshold 0.0261 as a vertical line, and the false-alarm (4.0%) and detection (58.3%) fractions annotated.

checks: A linear autoencoder with d_z = 3 is trained on centred data with squared error. What does it recover? -> The span of the top three principal components, not necessarily the components themselves.

How is the anomaly threshold chosen, and which error rate does that choice fix? -> At a high percentile of reconstruction errors on held-out normal data; it fixes the false-alarm rate (about 100 minus the percentile, in per cent); the detection rate must be measured on known anomalies.

sections.title: Variational autoencoders: the ELBO and the reparameterisation trick
sections.purpose: Derive the VAE objective from the latent-variable model, show exactly what the bound gives up, make its gradient computable, and explain and diagnose posterior collapse.
must_cover: Latent-variable model p_theta(x) = integral of p_theta(x|z) p(z) dz with prior p(z) = N(0, I). Direct maximum likelihood is intractable: the integral is over d_z dimensions and the posterior p_theta(z|x) is unknown.

ELBO by Jensen, written line by line: log p_theta(x) = log E_{q_phi(z|x)}[p_theta(x|z) p(z) / q_phi(z|x)] >= E_q[log p_theta(x|z)] - D_KL(q_phi(z|x) || p(z)). Name the two terms: reconstruction and the penalty that keeps codes near the prior.

ELBO as an identity: log p_theta(x) = ELBO + D_KL(q_phi(z|x) || p_theta(z|x)), derived from p(x) = p(x|z)p(z)/p(z|x) by taking the expectation under q. The gap is the KL to the true posterior; maximising over phi tightens the bound, maximising over theta raises the likelihood.
Amortised inference: one encoder network outputs (mu_phi(x), log sigma^2_phi(x)) for every x, instead of a separate optimisation of q for each data point.
Closed-form KL for a diagonal Gaussian against N(0, I): (1/2) sum_j (mu_j^2 + sigma_j^2 - log sigma_j^2 - 1), from Section 1's formula; independent dimensions add.

The gradient problem and its two answers: the score-function (REINFORCE) estimator E_q[f(z) grad_phi log q_phi(z)] is unbiased but high-variance; the reparameterisation z = mu_phi(x) + sigma_phi(x) * eps, eps ~ N(0, I), makes z a differentiable function of mu and sigma, so grad_phi E_eps[f(mu + sigma * eps)] = E_eps[grad_phi f(mu + sigma * eps)]; dz/dmu = 1, dz/dsigma = eps.

Decoder likelihoods: Bernoulli for intensities in [0, 1] (binary cross-entropy) or Gaussian N(x-hat, sigma_x^2 I) with -log p = ||x - x-hat||^2 / (2 sigma_x^2) + (d_x/2) log(2 pi sigma_x^2). The source's MSE-sum loss is the Gaussian with sigma_x^2 = 1/2, a wide noise model for [0, 1] pixels. sigma_x sets the exchange rate between reconstruction and KL; the beta-VAE (Higgins et al. 2017) weights the KL by beta.
Reproduce the source's VAE class (encoder to 2 d_z outputs split into mu and logvar, reparameterised sample, decoder, reconstruction plus closed-form KL), and state the likelihood choice explicitly.

Posterior collapse: q_phi(z|x) is close to p(z) for every x in some or all dimensions, and the decoder ignores z. Causes: a KL weight too large for the likelihood term (beta > 1, or a large implied sigma_x^2); a decoder that can model x without z (autoregressive decoders in text VAEs, Bowman et al. 2016). Diagnosis: KL per dimension; active units, the dimensions with Var_x(E_q[z_j]) > 0.01 (Burda et al. 2016). Fixes: KL warm-up from 0, free bits (Kingma et al. 2016), beta <= 1, a better-scaled likelihood. Warm-up cannot fix collapse that is the optimum of the chosen objective: in Lab 1, beta = 4 stays collapsed even with warm-up.

Lab 1 numbers (d_z = 8, Bernoulli decoder): beta = 0.5 gives KL 6.5 nats and 8 active units; beta = 1 gives 3.6 nats and 6 active; beta = 4 gives 0.00 nats, 0 active, and reconstruction 27.2 nats against 21.0 at beta = 1. The MSE-sum loss at beta = 1 gives KL 0.6 nats and 3 active units.

Why VAE samples are blurry: the decoder outputs the average of the plausible images for a code. VAEs are valued for their smooth, interpolable latent space (a latent design space in engineering terms) and as the compressor inside latent diffusion (Section 6).
worked_examples: A model where everything is exact: p(z) = N(0, 1), p(x|z) = N(z, 1), so p(x) = N(0, 2) and p(z|x) = N(x/2, 1/2). For x = 2: log p(x) = -(1/2) log(4 pi) - 1 = -2.2655. With q = N(1, 0.5), the true posterior: E_q[log p(x|z)] = -(1/2) log(2 pi) - (1/2)[(x - m)^2 + s^2] = -0.9189 - 0.75 = -1.6689; KL(q || p(z)) = (1/2)(1 + 0.5 - log 0.5 - 1) = 0.5966; ELBO = -2.2655 = log p(x), the bound is tight. With q = N(0, 1), a collapsed posterior equal to the prior: E_q[log p(x|z)] = -0.9189 - (1/2)(4 + 1) = -3.4189, KL = 0, ELBO = -3.4189, gap 1.1534 = KL(N(0, 1) || N(1, 0.5)), the number from Section 1.

Closed-form KL in two dimensions: mu = (1.0, -0.5), sigma = (0.5, 1.0). Per dimension (1/2)(1 + 0.25 + 1.3863 - 1) = 0.8181 and (1/2)(0.25 + 1 - 0 - 1) = 0.125; total 0.9431 nats. The first dimension pays mainly for its narrow variance (-log sigma^2 = 1.386), not for its mean.

Reparameterisation with the same mu and sigma and eps = (0.3, -1.2): z = mu + sigma * eps = (1.15, -1.70); dz/dmu = (1, 1), dz/dsigma = eps = (0.3, -1.2). The gradient reaches mu and sigma through an ordinary multiply and add.

Dashed red gradient arrows flow back through z to mu and sigma and, visibly, not into eps.

The exact example: on a z axis from -3 to 4, the prior N(0, 1), the true posterior N(1, 0.5), and beside it a stacked bar decomposing log p(x) = -2.27 into ELBO plus gap for q = posterior (gap 0) and q = prior (gap 1.15).

checks: What is the gap between log p(x) and the ELBO? -> D_KL(q_phi(z|x) || p_theta(z|x)), the KL from the approximate posterior to the true one.

Why can't you back-propagate through 'draw z from N(mu, sigma^2)' directly, and what does the reparameterisation change? -> Drawing a sample is not a differentiable function of mu and sigma; writing z = mu + sigma * eps with eps as an input makes z differentiable in both.

A VAE's KL term is 0.00 nats in every dimension. What do its samples look like, and why? -> All alike, roughly the average image: q equals the prior for every x, so z carries no information and the decoder ignores it.

sections.title: Generative adversarial networks
sections.purpose: Derive what the GAN game optimises, why its original loss stalls, why it collapses onto a few modes, and why diffusion displaced it for most new work.
must_cover: The game: min_G max_D V(G, D) = E_{x ~ p_data}[log D(x)] + E_{z ~ p(z)}[log(1 - D(G(z)))]; D outputs a probability through a sigmoid on a logit a.
Optimal discriminator derived pointwise: for fixed G, a log y + b log(1 - y) is maximised at y = a/(a + b), so D*(x) = p_data(x) / (p_data(x) + p_g(x)): the discriminator estimates a density ratio.
Substituting D*: V(G, D*) = -log 4 + 2 JSD(p_data || p_g), minimised (value -log 4) exactly when p_g = p_data.

Saturation: early in training D(G(z)) is near 0 and the gradient of log(1 - sigma(a)) with respect to the logit is -sigma(a), near 0; the non-saturating loss -log D(G(z)) has gradient -(1 - sigma(a)), near -1. Same fixed point, different dynamics.

Mode collapse: nothing in the loss rewards covering all of p_data; G can map many z to the few outputs D currently accepts; D adapts and G hops to other modes (Metz et al. 2017 show this on a ring of eight Gaussians). Diagnose with diversity measures (modes covered, nearest-neighbour distances from held-out data to samples, precision and recall), never with the loss.

Disjoint supports: when p_data and p_g sit on non-overlapping low-dimensional sets, the JSD is log 2 whatever their distance, so it carries no information about which way to move. The Wasserstein-1 (earth mover's) distance W(p, q) = inf over couplings gamma of E_{(x, y) ~ gamma} ||x - y|| does. Kantorovich-Rubinstein dual: W = sup over 1-Lipschitz f of E_p[f] - E_q[f], with a critic f. WGAN enforced the Lipschitz condition by weight clipping; WGAN-GP by a penalty lambda E[(||grad f(x-hat)|| - 1)^2] on interpolates; spectral normalisation is the other common stabiliser.

Where GANs stand, dated 'as of 2026': the fastest generators (one forward pass) and the first to produce photorealistic images; since about 2021 diffusion has replaced them for most new image work (Dhariwal and Nichol 2021) because it trains as a stable regression, covers the modes (its objective is a likelihood bound), conditions easily and scales. The adversarial loss survives as a term in image and audio codecs, in the autoencoder of latent diffusion (Rombach et al. train it with a patch-based adversarial term) and in distilling diffusion models to few steps.
Engineering uses: fast samplers for design-space exploration and data augmentation, super-resolution of fields; check coverage before trusting the samples.
worked_examples: Optimal discriminator on three points: p_data = (0.5, 0.5, 0), p_g = (0, 0.5, 0.5). D* = (1, 0.5, 0). V = 0.5 log 1 + 0.5 log 0.5 + 0.5 log 0.5 + 0.5 log 1 = -0.6931. Check: m = (0.25, 0.5, 0.25), JSD = (1/2)KL(p_data || m) + (1/2)KL(p_g || m) = 0.3466, and -log 4 + 2(0.3466) = -0.6931. With p_g = p_data, D* = 1/2 everywhere and V = -log 4 = -1.3863; with disjoint p_data = (1, 0) and p_g = (0, 1), V = 0 and JSD = log 2 = 0.6931, its maximum.

Saturation in numbers: at D(G(z)) = 0.01 (logit a = -4.6), d/da log(1 - sigma(a)) = -0.01 while d/da [-log sigma(a)] = -0.99. The non-saturating loss gives the generator a gradient 99 times larger at the moment it most needs one.

Disjoint supports: p_data a point mass at 0, p_g a point mass at theta. For every theta other than 0, JSD = log 2 = 0.693 and its gradient in theta is zero; W1 = |theta| with gradient sign(theta), pointing home from any distance.

figures.description: GAN training loop: noise z -> G -> fake samples; real samples from the data; both into D -> probability 'real'; two loss arrows, D's (classify real versus fake) and G's (fool D), annotated 'non-saturating: maximise log D(G(z))'.
One-dimensional picture: p_data with two bumps, p_g with one bump between them, and D*(x) = p_data / (p_data + p_g) as a dashed curve on a secondary axis from 0 to 1.

Mode collapse schematic, labelled as illustrative and not data (after Metz et al. 2017): a ring of eight Gaussian modes; GAN samples at four training snapshots sitting on one or two modes that change from snapshot to snapshot; beside it diffusion samples covering all eight.

checks: At a point where p_data = 0.3 and p_g = 0.1, what is D*? -> 0.3/0.4 = 0.75.

Why does the Jensen-Shannon divergence give the generator no direction when p_data and p_g sit on disjoint supports, and what does the Wasserstein-1 distance do instead? -> The JSD equals log 2 for any two disjoint distributions, however far apart they are, so its gradient is zero; W1 grows with the distance between them (|theta| for two point masses), so its gradient points p_g toward p_data.

sections.title: Diffusion I: the forward process and the training objective
sections.purpose: Build the forward noising process and its closed form, show how the schedule controls it, and derive the noise-prediction loss from the ELBO and from denoising score matching.
must_cover: Forward process: q(x_t | x_{t-1}) = N(sqrt(1 - beta_t) x_{t-1}, beta_t I) for t = 1..T; alpha_t = 1 - beta_t; alpha-bar_t = product over s <= t of alpha_s. The sqrt(1 - beta_t) factor keeps unit-variance data at unit variance.

Closed form q(x_t | x_0) = N(sqrt(alpha-bar_t) x_0, (1 - alpha-bar_t) I), derived by composing two steps (independent Gaussian noises add: alpha_t (1 - alpha-bar_{t-1}) + (1 - alpha_t) = 1 - alpha-bar_t) and induction. A training input is x_t = sqrt(alpha-bar_t) x_0 + sqrt(1 - alpha-bar_t) eps in one line, with no loop over t.

Schedules: Ho et al.'s linear beta from 1e-4 to 0.02 with T = 1000 (alpha-bar_T = 4.0e-5); the cosine schedule (Nichol and Dhariwal 2021) alpha-bar_t = f(t)/f(0) with f(t) = cos^2(((t/T + s)/(1 + s)) * pi/2), s = 0.008, beta_t clipped at 0.999 in the paper. Signal-to-noise ratio SNR(t) = alpha-bar_t / (1 - alpha-bar_t). Requirement: alpha-bar_T close to 0, so that x_T is close to N(0, I), where sampling starts.

The reverse conditional q(x_{t-1} | x_t, x_0) = N(mu-tilde_t, beta-tilde_t I) with mu-tilde_t = (sqrt(alpha-bar_{t-1}) beta_t / (1 - alpha-bar_t)) x_0 + (sqrt(alpha_t)(1 - alpha-bar_{t-1}) / (1 - alpha-bar_t)) x_t and beta-tilde_t = ((1 - alpha-bar_{t-1}) / (1 - alpha-bar_t)) beta_t. Stated, with 'complete the square in x_{t-1}' named as the skipped algebra.

The diffusion ELBO as a sum of per-step KLs between Gaussians (L_T + sum of L_{t-1} + L_0); with fixed variances each KL is a weighted squared difference of means; substituting x_0 = (x_t - sqrt(1 - alpha-bar_t) eps) / sqrt(alpha-bar_t) gives mu-tilde_t = (1/sqrt(alpha_t))(x_t - (beta_t / sqrt(1 - alpha-bar_t)) eps), so parameterising mu_theta the same way with eps_theta turns each term into a weighted ||eps - eps_theta(x_t, t)||^2. Ho et al. drop the weights: L_simple = E_{t, x_0, eps} ||eps - eps_theta(sqrt(alpha-bar_t) x_0 + sqrt(1 - alpha-bar_t) eps, t)||^2 (the source's equation).

The dropped weight with sigma_t^2 = beta_t is beta_t / (2 alpha_t (1 - alpha-bar_t)): 0.50 at t = 1, 0.010 at t = 100, 0.0055 at t = 500, 0.010 at t = 1000 for the linear schedule. Relative to the ELBO, L_simple moves emphasis away from the easiest, smallest-t steps.

The score view: grad_{x_t} log q(x_t | x_0) = -eps / sqrt(1 - alpha-bar_t), so an eps-predictor is a scaled score estimator, s_theta = -eps_theta / sqrt(1 - alpha-bar_t) (denoising score matching: Vincent 2011; Song and Ermon 2019). Tweedie's formula E[x_0 | x_t] = (x_t + (1 - alpha-bar_t) grad log p_t(x_t)) / sqrt(alpha-bar_t) means x-hat_0 = (x_t - sqrt(1 - alpha-bar_t) eps_theta) / sqrt(alpha-bar_t) is a posterior mean: an average, which is why denoising pure noise in one step gives a blur.
Why training is stable: a plain regression against a fixed target distribution, with no adversary.
Other parameterisations: predict x_0, or v = sqrt(alpha-bar) eps - sqrt(1 - alpha-bar) x_0 (Salimans and Ho 2022); the same information with different weighting over t.
The network: a U-Net (Module 03) or a transformer for images, an MLP in Lab 2; t enters through a sinusoidal embedding (the same construction as the positional encodings of Module 06).
worked_examples: Schedules in numbers, T = 1000: linear alpha-bar_t = 0.897, 0.524, 0.0786, 0.00335 and 4.0e-5 at t = 100, 250, 500, 750 and 1000; cosine 0.972, 0.847, 0.494, 0.144 and 2.4e-9. The linear schedule falls below alpha-bar = 0.01 (SNR -20 dB) at t = 674 and spends 33% of its steps there; the cosine schedule falls below it at t = 936 (6.5% of steps). Those steps are nearly pure noise and teach the model little.
One noising step in closed form: x_0 = 2.0, alpha-bar_t = 0.5, eps = -0.4: x_t = sqrt(0.5) * 2 + sqrt(0.5) * (-0.4) = 1.4142 - 0.2828 = 1.1314.

The optimal denoiser for Gaussian data: x_0 ~ N(2, 0.25). At alpha-bar_t = 0.5, p(x_t) = N(sqrt(0.5) * 2, 0.5 * 0.25 + 0.5) = N(1.4142, 0.625), and the optimal noise prediction is eps*(x_t) = sqrt(1 - alpha-bar)(x_t - 1.4142)/0.625. At x_t = 1.0, eps* = 0.7071 * (-0.4142)/0.625 = -0.4686, so x-hat_0 = (1.0 - 0.7071 * (-0.4686))/0.7071 = 1.8828, equal to E[x_0 | x_t] from Gaussian conditioning, 2 + (0.7071 * 0.25/0.625)(1.0 - 1.4142) = 1.8828. For Gaussian data the ideal denoiser is linear; for multimodal data the network must learn a nonlinear one.

alpha-bar_t (left axis, linear scale) and SNR in dB (right axis) against t for the linear and cosine schedules with T = 1000; a horizontal line at alpha-bar = 0.01; the region where the linear schedule is below it (t > 674) shaded.

One training step as a diagram: draw x_0 from the data, t uniform on {1..T}, eps ~ N(0, I) -> x_t = sqrt(alpha-bar_t) x_0 + sqrt(1 - alpha-bar_t) eps -> network eps_theta(x_t, t) -> squared error against eps.

checks: Why can training draw x_t directly instead of running t noising steps? -> A composition of Gaussian steps is Gaussian: q(x_t | x_0) = N(sqrt(alpha-bar_t) x_0, (1 - alpha-bar_t) I).

What does the network's noise prediction tell you about the clean data? -> x-hat_0 = (x_t - sqrt(1 - alpha-bar_t) eps_theta) / sqrt(alpha-bar_t), the posterior mean E[x_0 | x_t]; equivalently eps_theta is the score scaled by -sqrt(1 - alpha-bar_t).

In the diffusion explorer, set t = 500. Which schedule still shows the ring, and why? -> The cosine schedule (alpha-bar = 0.49, SNR about 0 dB); under the linear schedule alpha-bar = 0.079 and the ring is gone.

sections.title: Diffusion II: sampling, guidance, latent diffusion and cost
sections.purpose: Turn the trained noise predictor into a sampler, steer it with a condition, make it affordable in a latent space, and count what it costs at inference.
must_cover: Ancestral (DDPM) sampling: x_T ~ N(0, I); for t = T..1, x_{t-1} = (1/sqrt(alpha_t))(x_t - (beta_t / sqrt(1 - alpha-bar_t)) eps_theta(x_t, t)) + sigma_t z, z ~ N(0, I), z = 0 at the last step, sigma_t^2 = beta_t or beta-tilde_t. T network evaluations per sample.

The first step when beta_T is near 1: the factor 1/sqrt(alpha_T) is 31.6 for beta_T = 0.999 and multiplies any error in eps_theta. Lab 2 caps beta at 0.5 with T = 200 (alpha-bar_T = 6.8e-5, factor 1.41). Equivalent fix: compute x-hat_0, clip it to the data range, and take the posterior mean mu-tilde_t(x_t, x-hat_0).

DDIM (Song, Meng and Ermon 2021): a deterministic update x_{t'} = sqrt(alpha-bar_{t'}) x-hat_0 + sqrt(1 - alpha-bar_{t'}) eps_theta(x_t, t) on a strided subsequence of steps, with the same trained network. Lab 2's step sweep: precision distance 0.023 at 200 steps, 0.030 at 20, 0.045 at 5 and 1.57 at 1 (one step from pure noise returns a scaled-up posterior mean, far from the data).
Conditioning: feed c (a class, a text embedding, a low-resolution image, a measured boundary condition) to eps_theta(x_t, t, c).
Classifier guidance (Dhariwal and Nichol 2021) in one sentence: add the gradient of a noisy-input classifier's log p(c | x_t).

Classifier-free guidance (Ho and Salimans 2022): train one network with c replaced by a null token with probability p_uncond (0.1-0.2; 0.2 in Lab 2); sample with eps-tilde = eps_theta(x_t, null) + w [eps_theta(x_t, c) - eps_theta(x_t, null)]: w = 0 unconditional, w = 1 conditional, w > 1 extrapolates. Interpretation: grad log p(x | c) + (w - 1) grad log p(c | x), sharpening toward samples a classifier would label c. Two network evaluations per step. Convention warning: Ho and Salimans write (1 + w), so their w is this module's w minus 1.

The guidance trade-off measured in Lab 2 (1,000 samples of class 0): w = 0 puts 50% in the requested moon; w = 1 puts 100% there with recall distance 0.022; w = 3, 100% with recall 0.029; w = 7, 100% with recall 0.046 and precision worsening from 0.014 to 0.033. Fidelity is bought with diversity.

Latent diffusion (Rombach et al. 2022): train an autoencoder (KL-regularised, with perceptual and adversarial losses) that compresses, for example, a 512 x 512 x 3 image to a 64 x 64 x 4 latent (downsampling factor 8), run diffusion on the latent, decode once at the end.
Cost = steps x evaluations per step x cost per evaluation. Distillation to 1-4 steps: progressive distillation (Salimans and Ho 2022), consistency models (Song et al. 2023).

Engineering uses (generic): candidate geometries conditioned on requirements; imputing missing sensor channels by conditioning on the observed ones; super-resolving coarse simulation fields. Every generated design still goes through the solver and the checks.
worked_examples: Classifier-free guidance in two dimensions: eps_theta(x_t, null) = (0.2, -0.1), eps_theta(x_t, c) = (0.5, 0.3). w = 0 gives (0.2, -0.1); w = 1 gives (0.5, 0.3); w = 3 gives (0.2 + 3 * 0.3, -0.1 + 3 * 0.4) = (1.1, 1.1); w = 7.5 gives (2.45, 2.9). For w > 1 the guided prediction leaves the segment between the two estimates.
Latent compression: 512 x 512 x 3 = 786,432 values per image against 64 x 64 x 4 = 16,384 per latent: the denoiser processes 48 times fewer values at every step.
Inference cost: 50 sampling steps with classifier-free guidance = 100 network evaluations per image, against 1 for a GAN; a distilled 4-step sampler with the guidance folded into the student needs 4.

figures.description: Lab 2 reverse process: seven scatter panels of 2,000 samples at t = 200, 150, 100, 50, 20, 5 and 0, each annotated with the mean nearest-neighbour distance to the data (0.246, 0.234, 0.211, 0.134, 0.056, 0.025, 0.020): structure appears late.
Lab 2 guidance sweep: four panels of class-0 samples at w = 0, 1, 3 and 7 over a faint outline of both moons, each titled with the fraction in class 0 and the recall distance.

Latent diffusion pipeline with shapes on every arrow: image 512 x 512 x 3 -> encoder -> latent 64 x 64 x 4 -> diffusion loop (denoiser, with the condition c entering by cross-attention) -> decoder -> image.

checks: With p_uncond = 0.2 and w = 1, what does classifier-free guidance compute? -> The conditional prediction eps_theta(x_t, c) alone; guidance extrapolates only when w > 1.

Why is latent diffusion cheaper than pixel diffusion at the same image size? -> The denoiser runs at every step on a latent with 48 times fewer values (512 x 512 x 3 to 64 x 64 x 4); the decoder runs once.

sections.title: Graph neural networks I: message passing and the GCN
sections.purpose: Show how a network reads data whose structure is a graph, derive the GCN layer from message passing with symmetric normalisation, and compute one layer by hand on a fault tree.
must_cover: Graphs as data: G = (V, E) with n nodes, adjacency A in {0, 1}^{n x n}, degree matrix D, node features X in R^{n x d}, optional edge features. Examples: molecules, meshes, circuits, fault trees, SysML block diagrams, safety arguments in Goal Structuring Notation.

The constraint: node numbering is arbitrary, so layers must be permutation-equivariant, f(P A P^T, P X) = P f(A, X), and graph-level outputs permutation-invariant (sum, mean or max readout). An MLP on a flattened adjacency matrix breaks this and cannot take graphs of different sizes.

Message passing (Gilmer et al. 2017): m_v = AGG over u in N(v) of M(h_u, h_v, e_uv), h_v' = U(h_v, m_v). The source's form: h_v^(l+1) = phi(W_self h_v^(l) + sum over u in N(v) of W_nbr h_u^(l)). Weights are shared across nodes as a convolution shares them across positions (Module 03); L layers give an L-hop receptive field.

Why normalise: with sum aggregation a node of degree 50 receives messages 50 times larger than a leaf's, and repeated layers multiply by A's large eigenvalues, so features explode (on the 12-node tree with no normalisation the message-passing explorer's largest feature value reaches 1.22e4 after 8 steps).

GCN derivation (Kipf and Welling 2017): set W_self = W_nbr = W, add self-loops A-tilde = A + I, normalise symmetrically A-hat = D-tilde^{-1/2} A-tilde D-tilde^{-1/2}, so H^(l+1) = phi(A-hat H^(l) W^(l)) with entries A-hat_ij = 1/sqrt(d-tilde_i d-tilde_j). A-hat has largest eigenvalue 1 with eigenvector D-tilde^{1/2} 1, so repeated application neither explodes nor vanishes. Compare the random-walk normalisation D-tilde^{-1} A-tilde (mean aggregation). Kipf and Welling's motivation as a first-order approximation of a spectral filter with the 'renormalisation trick': one paragraph, no spectral theory required.

The source's code gcn_layer(A_hat, H, W) = relu(A_hat @ H @ W), and the edge-list form used in Lab 3: out_i = sum over j of A-hat_ij H_j, computed with index_add_ over (i, j, weight) triples; cost O(|E| d + n d d').

Fault trees as graphs: nodes are events and gates (OR, AND), edges join each input to its gate, features one-hot by type. A single point of failure is a basic event whose failure alone causes the top event: every gate on its path to the top is an OR. Deciding it needs information several hops away, which makes it the task of Lab 3.
Transductive (training and test nodes in one graph) versus inductive (new graphs at test time) learning; engineering models are usually inductive, so split by graph.
worked_examples: One GCN layer on a five-node fault tree: top event T (OR) with inputs G1 (AND) and basic event E3; G1 with inputs E1 and E2. Degrees with self-loops d-tilde = (T 3, G1 4, E1 2, E2 2, E3 2). Entries of A-hat: T-T 1/3 = 0.3333, T-G1 1/sqrt(12) = 0.2887, T-E3 1/sqrt(6) = 0.4082, G1-G1 0.25, G1-E1 1/sqrt(8) = 0.3536, E1-E1 0.5. Features [OR, AND, basic]: T (1, 0, 0), G1 (0, 1, 0), E1 to E3 (0, 0, 1). A-hat X: T (0.3333, 0.2887, 0.4082); G1 (0.2887, 0.25, 0.7071); E1 = E2 = (0, 0.3536, 0.5); E3 = (0.4082, 0, 0.5). After one layer (W = I, ReLU) E3's vector records that its gate is an OR and E1's that its gate is an AND: E3 is a single point of failure and E1 is not. For a deeper event the answer depends on gates further up, which needs more layers.
Normalisation check: the edge between a node with 3 neighbours and a leaf (1 neighbour), self-loops included, has weight 1/sqrt(4 * 2) = 0.354; unnormalised it would be 1.

figures.description: The five-node fault tree drawn top-down with gate shapes labelled OR and AND and circles for basic events; beside it the 5 x 5 matrix A-hat with its entries and the 5 x 3 matrix A-hat X with E3's and E1's rows highlighted.

Message passing for one node: neighbour feature vectors as arrows into the centre node, each multiplied by W and the weight 1/sqrt(d-tilde_i d-tilde_j), summed with the node's own transformed vector, then a nonlinearity; a side panel shades the two-hop receptive field of a basic event after two layers.

checks: Why must a GNN layer be permutation-equivariant? -> Node numbering is arbitrary; renumbering the nodes must renumber the outputs and change nothing else.
How many layers does a GCN need before a basic event at depth 3 can receive information from the top event? -> Three; each layer extends the receptive field by one hop.

sections.title: Graph neural networks II: attention, depth limits and engineering graphs
sections.purpose: Weight neighbours by learned attention, explain why GNNs stay shallow and what they cannot distinguish, handle directed and typed edges, and map the family onto engineering graphs.
must_cover: Graph attention (Velickovic et al. 2018): e_vu = LeakyReLU(a^T [W h_v || W h_u]), alpha_vu = softmax over u in N(v) and v itself of e_vu, h_v' = phi(sum_u alpha_vu W h_u); multi-head attention with concatenation or averaging. A transformer layer (Module 06) is attention over the complete graph plus positions; GAT restricts it to the edges.

Over-smoothing derived: for a connected graph with self-loops, A-hat^k X -> u u^T X as k grows, with u = D-tilde^{1/2} 1 / ||D-tilde^{1/2} 1||, because A-hat u = u (check: D-tilde^{-1/2} A-tilde 1 = D-tilde^{-1/2} d-tilde = D-tilde^{1/2} 1) and every other eigenvalue has |lambda| < 1. The difference decays as |lambda_2|^k; every node's vector becomes sqrt(d-tilde_i) times one common vector, so only degree survives (Li, Han and Wu 2018).
Without self-loops a tree is bipartite, A-hat has eigenvalue -1, and features oscillate between the two colour classes instead of converging (an edge case in the message-passing explorer).

Depth in practice: 2-4 layers is typical. Lab 3's plain GCN predicts the majority class for every event at 8 and 16 layers; residual updates H <- H + phi(A-hat H W) restore about 0.95-0.97. Other fixes: normalisation layers, jumping-knowledge connections, fewer but wider layers.
Over-squashing (Alon and Yahav 2021): an exponentially growing neighbourhood squeezed through bottleneck edges into a fixed-size vector, so long-range dependencies suffer.

Expressivity: with identical initial features, message passing cannot separate graphs that the 1-Weisfeiler-Lehman test cannot (Xu et al. 2019, where GIN with sum aggregation reaches that bound). Example: one 6-cycle against two triangles. Fixes: structural features (degree, cycle counts), positional encodings, random node identifiers.

Directed and typed edges: fault trees are directed (input to gate) and gates have types; a symmetric A-hat mixes a node's gate with its siblings and its own inputs. A relational GCN (Schlichtkrull et al. 2018) gives each edge type and direction its own weight matrix. Lab 3: the undirected GCN tops out around 0.94-0.96 on single points of failure; a direction-aware layer reaches 1.000 at four layers.

Engineering graphs: molecular property prediction from the bond graph; learned simulators on meshes, MeshGraphNets (Pfaff et al. 2021), with encode-process-decode, mesh edges carrying relative positions, trained to step a PDE in time; system models, where a fault tree, a GSN safety argument and a SysML model are graphs, and a network that reads them as graphs rather than flattened text is the natural tool for checking or completing them.
Graph-level tasks: pool node vectors by sum or mean for a whole-graph label (for example, whether a tree's top-event probability exceeds a target).
worked_examples: Attention weights: a node with three neighbours whose scores are e = (0.5, 1.0, -0.2): exp(e) = (1.6487, 2.7183, 0.8187), sum 5.1857, alpha = (0.318, 0.524, 0.158). The best-scoring neighbour gets half the weight; a GCN would have weighted the three by degree alone.

Over-smoothing on Section 7's five-node tree: the eigenvalues of A-hat are 1, 0.7655, 0.5, 0.0974 and -0.2795. The mean pairwise cosine similarity of the rows of A-hat^k X is 0.846 at k = 1, 0.933 at 2, 0.976 at 4, 0.997 at 8 and 1.000 at 16, as |lambda_2|^k = 0.586, 0.343, 0.118 and 0.014 (k = 2, 4, 8, 16) predicts. The limit u u^T X has u proportional to sqrt(d-tilde) = (sqrt 3, 2, sqrt 2, sqrt 2, sqrt 2).

A 1-WL failure: in a 6-cycle and in two triangles every node has degree 2 and the same feature, so every message-passing step gives every node the same vector in both graphs; no number of layers separates a graph with one 6-cycle from a graph with two 3-cycles.

figures.description: GAT on one node: three neighbour arrows with thickness proportional to alpha = (0.318, 0.524, 0.158), beside the same node under a GCN with weights set by degree.

Over-smoothing curves from the message-passing explorer's reference numbers: mean pairwise cosine similarity of A-hat^k X against k = 0..40 on the 12-node cooling-system tree for symmetric normalisation (0.455 at k = 0; 0.856, 0.967, 0.993, 0.999 at k = 1, 4, 8, 16), random-walk normalisation, and symmetric normalisation without self-loops (oscillating, settling near 0.976).
Two graphs message passing cannot tell apart: a hexagon and two triangles, all nodes the same colour, with the identical node vectors after one and two rounds shown side by side.

checks: As k grows, what does A-hat^k X converge to, and what information is left? -> u u^T X with u proportional to D-tilde^{1/2} 1: every row is one common vector scaled by sqrt(d-tilde_i), so only degree survives.

Why does Lab 3's direction-aware model beat the GCN on single points of failure? -> The property depends only on the gates above an event; separate weights for messages from the gate and from the inputs let the model pass 'all gates above are OR' downward, while a symmetric A-hat mixes it with information from siblings and inputs.

In the explorer, set the normalisation to 'none'. What happens to the feature values, and why? -> They explode. With P = A-tilde, each step multiplies the features' component along the top eigenvector of A-tilde by its eigenvalue, 3.392, so the growth factor after 8 steps is 3.392^8 = 1.75e4. The explorer's readout, the largest single feature value at k = 8, is 1.22e4: smaller than the growth factor because only part of the one-hot starting features lies along that eigenvector. Unnormalised sums explode.

sections.title: Physics-informed neural networks
sections.purpose: Train a network to satisfy a known differential equation by penalising its residual, show the loss terms and how to balance them, and be honest about when this beats a classical solver and when it does not.
must_cover: The problem shape: the equation is known and the data are sparse; represent the solution by a network u_theta(x, t).

The composite loss, reproducing the source's equation: a data term (1/N_d) sum (u_theta(x_i, t_i) - u_i)^2, a residual term (1/N_c) sum (N[u_theta](x_j, t_j))^2 at collocation points, and a boundary/initial term (1/N_b) sum (B[u_theta](x_k, t_k))^2, with weights lambda_d, lambda_r, lambda_b.

Derivatives of the network with respect to its inputs by reverse-mode autodiff (Module 02): torch.autograd.grad(u, t, grad_outputs=torch.ones_like(u), create_graph=True)[0], applied twice for u''. create_graph=True records the derivative computation so the loss on u'' can itself be differentiated with respect to theta. Smooth activations (tanh), because ReLU's second derivative is zero almost everywhere.

The worked ODE: u'' + 2 zeta w0 u' + w0^2 u = 0 with u(0) = 1, u'(0) = 0; residual r(t) = u_theta'' + 2 zeta w0 u_theta' + w0^2 u_theta; exact solution u(t) = exp(-zeta w0 t)[cos(wd t) + (zeta w0/wd) sin(wd t)], wd = w0 sqrt(1 - zeta^2). Lab 4 uses w0 = 2 pi rad/s (1 Hz) and zeta = 0.1 on [0, 2] s.

The trivial solution: u = 0 has zero residual for a homogeneous equation, and only the initial or boundary terms exclude it. At initialisation in dimensional units the residual loss is 52.5 against an initial-condition loss of 1.36; the optimiser reduces the large term first and lands on zero (Lab 4: relative error 0.998 with lambda_ic = 1).

Three fixes, measured in Lab 4: raise lambda_ic to 100 (error 0.004 after 10,000 steps); non-dimensionalise with t-hat = w0 t so the equation becomes u'' + 2 zeta u' + u = 0 with coefficients of order 1 (error 0.0004; initial residual loss 0.034); impose the conditions by construction, u_theta(t) = 1 + t^2 N_theta(t) (Lagaris et al. 1998), which removes the trivial solution but not the poor scaling (error 0.09 in dimensional units after 10,000 steps).

Inverse problems: unknown coefficients become trainable parameters (zeta through log zeta). Lab 4 recovers zeta = 0.0987 from 12 noisy readings (true 0.1), matching a least-squares fit of the closed form (0.0977 +/- 0.0015). The PINN earns its cost where there is no closed form, or where a whole field must be recovered from a PDE.

Failure modes beyond the trivial solution: stiffness and multiscale behaviour, with loss terms of very different sizes (Wang, Teng and Perdikaris 2021 analyse the gradient imbalance and propose adaptive weights); spectral bias, networks fitting low frequencies first (Rahaman et al. 2019), so oscillatory or sharp solutions converge slowly (Fourier-feature inputs, Tancik et al. 2020); long time windows fitted out of causal order (time-marching over subintervals helps); PDE regimes where training fails outright (Krishnapriyan et al. 2021, convection at high speed); hand-tuned loss weights; and ill-posed set-ups, where a missing boundary condition leaves infinitely many solutions (exercise e12).

The honest comparison: for forward problems on a known geometry a finite-element or finite-difference solver is usually faster and more accurate; claims for learned PDE solvers should be checked against strong classical baselines (McGreivy and Hakim 2024). PINNs earn their place in data assimilation and inverse problems (sparse measurements plus a known equation), on awkward domains without a mesh, and where a differentiable model of the parameters is wanted.
worked_examples: The residual of a near miss, by hand, with Lab 4's values w0 = 2 pi rad/s and zeta = 0.1: try the undamped solution u(t) = cos(w0 t), which meets both initial conditions exactly. u'' = -w0^2 cos(w0 t) cancels w0^2 u, leaving r(t) = -2 zeta w0^2 sin(w0 t) = -0.8 pi^2 sin(2 pi t) = -7.90 sin(2 pi t). At t = 0.25 s, r = -7.90; over [0, 2] s, two whole periods, the mean of r^2 is (0.8 pi^2)^2 / 2 = 31.2 (31.0 on Lab 4's 200 evenly spaced collocation points). The trivial solution u = 0 has zero residual and an initial-condition loss of (0 - 1)^2 + 0^2 = 1. With lambda_ic = 1 the loss therefore rates a curve that only lacks the damping 31 times worse than zero: the trivial-solution failure in miniature. With lambda_ic = 100, zero costs 100 against the near miss's 31.2 and the ranking flips, which is Lab 4's first fix.

Why non-dimensionalising works: with t-hat = w0 t the equation becomes u'' + 2 zeta u' + u = 0, with coefficients 1, 2 zeta = 0.2 and 1. The same near miss, u = cos(t-hat), leaves r = -0.2 sin(t-hat) and a mean r^2 of 0.02 over the same two periods, against 1.0 for zero: the loss now ranks it 50 times better than the trivial solution, with no weight to tune. In dimensional units every term of the residual carries up to w0^2 = 39.5, so a network output of order 1 gives residuals of order 40 and a residual loss of order 10^3, against an initial-condition loss of order 1; Lab 4's freshly initialised network starts at 52.5 against 1.36 (Figure 5.23). Halving the output halves the residual; sending it to zero removes the residual entirely.

Lab 4 results on one time axis from 0 to 2 s: the exact solution; the PINN with lambda_ic = 1 in dimensional units (flat near zero); lambda_ic = 100 and the non-dimensional PINN (on top of the exact curve); the 12 noisy readings and the inverse-problem fit with zeta = 0.099.

checks: Why does a PINN for a homogeneous equation need its initial or boundary terms to avoid u = 0? -> Zero satisfies the equation exactly; only the conditions rule it out, and if their weight is small the optimiser finds zero first.

What does create_graph=True do in the derivative call? -> It records the derivative computation, so the loss built from u' and u'' can be differentiated with respect to the network weights; without it the second derivative and the residual's gradient are not available.

sections.title: Neural operators and surrogate models
sections.purpose: Explain how a network learns the map from an input function to a solution field across a family of problems, and how to judge such a surrogate before using it.
must_cover: Operator learning: G maps a to u, where a is a coefficient field, a forcing, a boundary condition or a geometry and u is the solution; trained on pairs (a_i, u_i) produced by a solver; one forward pass per new instance.

Surrogates in engineering terms: response surfaces, kriging and Gaussian-process surrogates, reduced-order models by proper orthogonal decomposition, u(y) approx sum_k c_k phi_k(y). Neural operators are the same idea with learned bases.

DeepONet (Lu et al. 2021): a branch net b(a(y_1), ..., a(y_m)) in R^p reads the input function at m fixed sensors, a trunk net t(y) in R^p reads the query point, and G(a)(y) approx sum_k b_k(a) t_k(y) plus a bias. Its theory goes back to Chen and Chen's 1995 universal approximation theorem for operators. The trunk plays the role of POD modes, the branch of their coefficients.

Fourier neural operator (Li et al. 2021): lift v_0 = P(a); Fourier layers v_{l+1} = sigma(W v_l + F^{-1}(R_l . F(v_l))) keeping the lowest k_max modes; project u = Q(v_L). The spectral weights do not depend on the grid, so the trained model can be evaluated at another resolution, with caveats (aliasing; the training distribution still bounds validity).

Validity: a surrogate is valid on the distribution of inputs it was trained on; extrapolation in geometry, material or load regime is unquantified. Before use: check new inputs against the training ranges, validate against fresh solver runs where the surrogate will be used, report the error per regime and a validity domain. Reported speed-ups mean something only against a solver run to the same accuracy (McGreivy and Hakim 2024).

The practical route to a fast approximate finite-element solver for a family of designs: trained on a few thousand solver runs, it answers a new member of the family in one forward pass, and only inside the family those runs covered.
On unstructured meshes, graph-network simulators (MeshGraphNets, Section 8) play the operator role.
worked_examples: Parameters of one 1D Fourier layer with width 32 and k_max = 16 retained modes: the complex tensor R has 16 x 32 x 32 = 16,384 entries, 32,768 real parameters; the pointwise W has 32 x 32 + 32 = 1,056. The spectral part dominates and does not grow with the grid.

DeepONet shapes for a 1D problem: the input function at m = 100 sensors -> branch net -> p = 64 coefficients; a query point y -> trunk net -> 64 basis values; the output at y is their dot product. A field of 10,000 query points costs one branch evaluation and 10,000 trunk evaluations.

figures.description: DeepONet: an input function a(y) drawn as a curve with m sensor dots -> branch net -> vector b; a query point y -> trunk net -> vector t; dot product -> G(a)(y). Beside it, the POD analogy: modes phi_k(y) as curves and coefficients c_k as bars.
One Fourier layer: v -> FFT -> keep the k_max lowest modes -> multiply by R -> inverse FFT; in parallel v -> W (pointwise linear); sum -> nonlinearity sigma.

checks: What does a trained neural operator take as input, and what does it return? -> A function (a coefficient field, forcing or boundary condition, sampled at points) and the corresponding solution function, for any member of the trained family, in one forward pass.

Name two checks before using a surrogate trained on solver output for a new design. -> That the new input lies inside the training ranges; and validation against fresh solver runs in the region where it will be used, with the error reported per regime.

sections.title: Contrastive and self-supervised learning
sections.purpose: Show how an encoder learns useful features from unlabelled data by telling a positive pair apart from negatives, derive InfoNCE as a classification loss, and show that the augmentations decide what is learned.
must_cover: The problem: labels are expensive and structure is free. A pretext task needs no labels; the representation is judged by a linear probe trained on a few labels.

InfoNCE derived as softmax cross-entropy (the source's equation): among N candidates, one positive and N - 1 negatives, with scores sim(z_i, z_j)/tau, L = -log[exp(sim(z_i, z_i+)/tau) / sum_j exp(sim(z_i, z_j)/tau)] is the cross-entropy of identifying the positive. sim is the cosine similarity of L2-normalised embeddings; the temperature tau sharpens the distribution.
The mutual-information view (van den Oord et al. 2018): I(x; x+) >= log N - L_InfoNCE, so the estimate can never exceed log N; more negatives (bigger batches) allow larger values.

SimCLR (Chen et al. 2020): two augmentations of each of the B inputs in a batch give 2B views; each view's positive is its twin and the other 2B - 2 views are negatives, so InfoNCE runs over N = 2B - 1 candidates per view (the NT-Xent loss). A projection head g sits on top of the representation h; probe h, not z, because the head learns to discard what the augmentations vary (Lab 5: probe on z 0.61 against h 0.93 with 5 labels per class).

Alignment and uniformity (Wang and Isola 2020): the loss pulls positives together and spreads all embeddings over the sphere. Collapsed embeddings (all equal) make every candidate equally likely and give the loss log(2B - 1) = log N, so the bound certifies no information; the negatives prevent it. Non-contrastive methods such as BYOL (Grill et al. 2020) avoid negatives with asymmetric networks.

The augmentations are the supervision: they say which differences the encoder must ignore. Lab 5: removing the time-shift augmentation drops the 5-label probe from 0.93 to 0.58, near the untrained encoder's 0.49.

An augmentation removes task information only if the classes differ in nothing it leaves intact. Cases where it does: 180-degree rotations make 6 and 9 the same digit; colour jitter removes the colour that identifies corrosion. In Lab 5 a 16-fold gain range did not hurt, because the classes also differ in harmonic ratios and signal-to-noise ratio.

CLIP (Radford et al. 2021): image and text encoders trained with a symmetric InfoNCE over a batch of B image-caption pairs (a B x B similarity matrix with positives on the diagonal, each row and each column an InfoNCE over B candidates) on 400 million pairs; zero-shot classification by embedding prompts such as 'a photo of a {label}' and taking the nearest; the embeddings behind text-to-image conditioning and many retrieval systems (retrieval-augmented generation is covered in the AI Agents series).

Masked modelling, the other branch: hide part of the input and predict it. BERT's masked tokens (Module 06), masked autoencoders for images with 75% of patches hidden (He et al. 2022); next-token prediction, the objective of Modules 07 and 08, is self-supervised in the same sense.

The general lesson (source): a pretext task with no labels can produce a representation that transfers to tasks with few labels. Engineering use: pretrain on months of unlabelled sensor logs, then fit a classifier on a handful of labelled faults; embeddings for retrieving similar past incidents or documents.
worked_examples: InfoNCE with N = 4 candidates and cosine similarities s = (0.9, 0.2, 0.1, -0.3), positive first. tau = 1: the positive's probability is e^0.9 / (e^0.9 + e^0.2 + e^0.1 + e^-0.3) = 2.460/5.527 = 0.445; loss 0.810; mutual-information bound log 4 - 0.810 = 0.577 nats. tau = 0.1: logits (9, 2, 1, -3), the positive's probability 0.9987, loss 0.0013, bound 1.385, essentially log 4 = 1.386: the bound is capped at log N.

Lab 5 in numbers (linear probe with 5 / 20 / 100 labels per class): raw waveform 0.376 / 0.447 / 0.485; FFT magnitude 0.790 / 0.890 / 0.975; untrained encoder 0.494 / 0.733 / 0.882; contrastive encoder 0.929 / 0.989 / 0.996. With 5 labels per class the pretrained features beat the classical spectral features by 14 points; with 100 the gap is 2 points.

figures.description: SimCLR pipeline: one vibration window -> two augmentations (time shift, gain, noise) -> shared encoder f -> h -> projection head g -> z on a unit circle; the positive pair pulled together, other batch members pushed apart; an arrow from h to 'linear probe'.

CLIP's B x B similarity matrix for a batch of B image-caption pairs with the diagonal highlighted as positives; row-wise and column-wise softmax arrows showing the two directions of the symmetric loss.

checks: What is the largest value the InfoNCE lower bound on mutual information can reach with N candidates? -> log N; with 256 candidates, 5.55 nats.

Why does SimCLR evaluate the representation before the projection head? -> The head learns to discard what the augmentations vary, which can include information the downstream task needs; h keeps more (0.93 against 0.61 in Lab 5 with 5 labels per class).

sections.title: Mixture of experts
sections.purpose: Show how routing each input to a few of many experts separates parameter count from compute, count both on a published configuration, and explain the routing failures.
must_cover: The layer (the source's equation): y = sum over e in top-k(g(x)) of g_e(x) FFN_e(x), with router g(x) = softmax(W_r x), k = 1 or 2, and the selected weights renormalised to sum to 1. In a transformer (Module 06) it replaces the feed-forward block, an MLP applied to each token; explain this in one sentence here, since Module 06 comes next.

Origins: Jacobs, Jordan, Nowlan and Hinton (1991), adaptive mixtures of local experts, a soft gate choosing among regressors, familiar to engineers who switch models between operating regimes; Shazeer et al. (2017), the sparsely-gated layer with noisy top-k gating.
Parameters against compute: parameters grow with E, compute per token with k. Count both on Mixtral 8x7B's published configuration.

Routing collapse: a feedback loop. An expert that receives more tokens gets more gradient, improves, is chosen more; the starved ones never improve. Symptom: most tokens on one or two experts. Load-balancing loss (Switch Transformer, Fedus et al. 2022): L_bal = lambda_bal * E * sum_e f_e P_e, where f_e is the fraction of tokens dispatched to expert e and P_e the mean router probability for e; its minimum is 1 (times lambda_bal) at uniform routing; Switch used lambda_bal = 0.01.
Capacity: each expert processes at most capacity factor x (tokens / E) tokens per batch; overflow tokens are dropped (passed on through the residual connection), a source of silent quality loss.

Other difficulties (source): communication between GPUs when experts are spread across them; instability early in training. A recent alternative: fine-grained plus shared experts and bias-based, auxiliary-loss-free balancing in DeepSeek-V3 (671B parameters in total, 37B active per token). LLM-scale MoE engineering is Module 08's.
Specialisation is less semantic than the name suggests: the Mixtral authors report no obvious assignment of experts by topic.
Serving cost: every expert must be in memory although each token uses only k of them (Module 10).
worked_examples: Mixtral 8x7B's published configuration: 32 layers, d = 4096, SwiGLU experts with d_ff = 14,336, 8 experts, top-2 routing, attention with 32 query heads and 8 key-value heads of 128 dimensions, vocabulary 32,000 with untied input and output embeddings. Per expert 3 x 4096 x 14,336 = 176.2M parameters; all experts of all layers 8 x 32 x 176.2M = 45.1B. Attention per layer 4096 x 4096 + 2 x 4096 x 1024 + 4096 x 4096 = 41.9M, so 1.34B in all; embeddings 2 x 32,000 x 4096 = 0.26B. Total about 46.7B; active per token 2 x 32 x 176.2M = 11.3B + 1.34B + 0.26B = about 12.9B. The paper reports 47B total and 13B active. (Router and normalisation weights, about 1M, are left out.)

Load-balancing loss with E = 4: collapsed routing f = (1, 0, 0, 0) with mean router probabilities P = (0.7, 0.1, 0.1, 0.1) gives E sum f_e P_e = 4 x 0.7 = 2.8; uniform routing f = P = (0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25) gives 4 x 4 x 0.0625 = 1.0. The loss is 2.8 times its minimum, and its gradient through P moves router probability toward the starved experts.

figures.description: An MoE layer in place of the feed-forward block: token vector -> router (softmax over 8 experts drawn as a bar chart) -> the top-2 experts highlighted and the other six greyed -> weighted sum -> residual add; a side note 'parameters: 8 FFNs; compute: 2 FFNs'.

checks: A model has 8 experts per layer and routes each token to 2. How does its per-token FFN compute compare with a dense model whose FFN is one expert? -> About twice (two experts run), while its FFN parameters are eight times as many.

What does the load-balancing loss measure, and what is its minimum? -> E sum f_e P_e, how far the token fractions and router probabilities are concentrated on the same experts; its minimum is 1, at uniform routing.
