sections.title: Choosing a family
sections.purpose: Turn the module into decisions: which family fits which engineering need, what baseline it must beat first, and what it costs.
must_cover: The source's table, every row kept, extended with two columns, 'first baseline to beat' and 'main cost or risk': compress, denoise, detect anomalies in unlabelled data -> autoencoder (PCA and its Q statistic; misses anomalies that resemble normal data); a smooth latent space to sample or interpolate designs -> VAE, diffusion (PCA plus a Gaussian; VAE samples blur, diffusion is slow to sample); the best sample quality with conditioning -> diffusion (a GAN or VAE; tens to hundreds of evaluations per sample); the fastest generator -> GAN (diffusion distilled to a few steps; mode collapse); data on a graph or mesh -> GNN (hand-made graph features or the obvious structural rule, e.g. the leaf rule; over-smoothing, edge direction); a known PDE and sparse data, or an inverse problem -> PINN (a classical solver wrapped in a least-squares fit; trivial solutions, stiffness); a fast surrogate for a solver across a family of inputs -> neural operator (a Gaussian-process or POD surrogate, and the solver itself; validity limited to the training family); representations without labels -> contrastive, masked prediction (spectral or engineered features, PCA; the augmentations decide what is learned); capacity without proportional compute -> mixture of experts (a dense model of the same active size; routing collapse, memory).

Three walk-throughs: (1) vibration monitoring of a pump fleet with no fault labels -> an autoencoder on normal data with a percentile threshold against the PCA Q-statistic baseline, then contrastive pretraining once a few faults are labelled (Lab 5); (2) candidate bracket geometries for a given load case -> conditional diffusion, in a latent space if the geometry is an image or voxel grid, every candidate checked by the solver; (3) stress fields across a family of perforated plates -> a neural operator or mesh GNN trained on solver runs, valid only for the hole sizes and loads it saw.
The series rule: state the baseline first; a model that does not beat it has learned nothing useful.
worked_examples: The labs as evidence: Lab 1's autoencoder beats PCA's Q statistic on held-out 9s (AUC 0.952 against 0.791); Lab 3's GCN beats the plausible 'gate is OR' rule (0.551) and the majority class (0.838) only from 3 layers on; Lab 5's contrastive features beat FFT magnitudes with 5 labels per class (0.929 against 0.790) and gain only 2 points with 100 (0.996 against 0.975); Lab 4's PINN matches, and does not beat, a closed-form fit (zeta 0.0987 against 0.0977).

figures.description: Decision flow: 'Is the data a graph or mesh?' -> GNN; 'Is there a governing equation?' -> PINN (sparse data, inverse problem) or neural operator (many solver runs, many queries); 'Do you need to generate?' -> diffusion (quality, conditioning), GAN (speed), VAE (latent space); 'Are labels scarce?' -> contrastive or masked pretraining; 'Need capacity at fixed compute?' -> MoE. Each leaf lists its first baseline in small type.

checks: You have a known heat-conduction PDE, 15 thermocouple readings and one unknown conductivity. Which family, and what baseline? -> A PINN, as an inverse problem; the baseline is a classical solver wrapped in a least-squares fit of the conductivity.
sections.from_source: Source section 8, the 'Choosing' table, all nine rows kept.
sections.new_material: The baseline and cost columns; three engineering walk-throughs; the decision-flow figure; the labs' numbers as evidence.

what_goes_wrong: VAE samples all look alike and the KL term reads 0.00 nats in every dimension -> posterior collapse: the KL weight is too strong for the likelihood term (beta > 1, or an MSE-sum loss that implies sigma_x^2 = 1/2 on [0, 1] pixels), or the decoder can model x without z -> use beta <= 1 with a properly scaled likelihood, warm the KL weight up from 0 or use free bits, and monitor KL per dimension and active units (Lab 1: beta = 4 leaves 0 of 8 active).

An autoencoder anomaly detector with a high AUC misses many real faults in service -> AUC averages over all thresholds, and anomalies that resemble normal data reconstruct well -> report the detection rate at the operating threshold (Lab 1: AUC 0.95 but 58% detected at 4% false alarms), compare with the PCA Q-statistic baseline, evaluate on known faults, and recalibrate the threshold when operating conditions change.

A GAN that 'trained fine' produces the same six images -> mode collapse: nothing in the adversarial loss rewards covering the data -> measure diversity (modes covered, recall-style nearest-neighbour distances from held-out data to samples), not only sample quality; stabilise with a gradient penalty or spectral normalisation, or use a diffusion model.

Diffusion samples look washed out and never reach extreme values, or sampling blows up on the first reverse step -> a schedule endpoint is wrong: alpha-bar_T far from 0 (Ho et al.'s beta range with T = 200 instead of 1,000 leaves alpha-bar_T = 0.13), so sampling starts from noise the network never saw; or beta_T near 1 (the cosine clip at 0.999), so the first update multiplies errors by 1/sqrt(alpha_T) = 31.6 and guidance amplifies them -> check alpha-bar_T and the largest beta before training; use a cosine schedule or zero-terminal-SNR rescaling; cap beta (0.5 in Lab 2) or clip x-hat_0 to the data range.

Samples are blurred or off the data with a fast sampler, or oversaturated and all alike with strong guidance -> too few sampling steps (Lab 2: DDIM precision distance 0.023 at 200 steps, 0.045 at 5, 1.57 at 1) or too large a guidance scale (recall distance 0.022 at w = 1, 0.046 at w = 7) -> use 20-50 DDIM steps or a distilled sampler, and choose w on a diversity measure as well as on appearance.

A generative model produces near-copies of training items -> memorisation, more likely with small or duplicated training sets and long training -> deduplicate the data, compare each sample's distance to its nearest training item with held-out distances, and give generated designs the same checks as any other (Carlini et al. 2023).

A GNN of ten layers gives every node the same features and predicts one class -> over-smoothing: repeated averaging drives all node vectors to one direction at rate |lambda_2|^k, and a deep plain stack also trains poorly -> use 2-4 layers or residual connections (Lab 3: 16 plain layers give 0.838, the majority class; with residuals about 0.95-0.97) and measure feature similarity layer by layer.

A GNN plateaus on a property that depends on edge direction or type, such as what lies above a node in a fault tree -> a symmetric normalised adjacency mixes parents, children and siblings -> give each edge direction or type its own weights (relational GCN) or add edge features (Lab 3: about 0.94-0.96 undirected against 1.000 direction-aware).

A GNN scores well in evaluation and badly on new graphs -> nodes of the same graph were split between training and test, so test nodes' neighbourhoods were seen in training -> split by graph (whole fault trees, whole meshes) whenever the model will meet new graphs.

A PINN converges to u = 0, or to a smooth curve that ignores the initial or boundary data -> zero satisfies the homogeneous equation and the condition terms are outweighed (Lab 4: residual loss 52.5 against 1.36 at the start, final error 0.998) -> non-dimensionalise (error 0.0004), raise the condition weights (0.004), or impose the conditions by construction.

A PINN fits slow trends but not oscillations, sharp fronts or late times, or a small residual hides a wrong answer -> spectral bias, stiffness and loss imbalance, or an ill-posed set-up (exercise e12: without boundary conditions the heat equation has infinitely many solutions, and the PINN found one with error 0.82 at a residual of 4e-5) -> Fourier-feature inputs, adaptive loss weights, time-marching over subintervals, a check that the problem is fully posed, or a classical solver, usually faster and more accurate for forward problems.

A neural operator or other surrogate gives confident, wrong answers for a new design -> the input lies outside the family it was trained on (another geometry family, load regime or material) -> check inputs against the training ranges, validate against fresh solver runs where the surrogate is used, and report the error per regime and a validity domain.

A contrastive encoder is useless for the downstream task, or its loss sits at log(2B - 1) for a batch of B ->the augmentations removed the information the task needs (a 180-degree rotation makes 6 and 9 one class; colour jitter removes the colour of corrosion), or the embeddings collapsed -> choose augmentations from the task's real invariances, check per-class probe accuracy, and remember that the augmentations are the supervision (Lab 5: without the time shift 0.58 instead of 0.93).

A mixture-of-experts layer sends most tokens to one or two experts -> routing collapse from rich-get-richer feedback -> add a load-balancing loss or bias-based balancing, and monitor per-expert token fractions and the number of dropped tokens.

labs.title: Autoencoders, a VAE and an anomaly detector on 8x8 digits
labs.goal: Compare a nonlinear autoencoder with PCA, train the source's VAE and inspect its latent space, cause posterior collapse on purpose, and build a reconstruction-error anomaly detector with an honestly chosen threshold.
labs.data: scikit-learn built-in load_digits (1,797 images of 8x8 pixels with values 0-16; ships with the package, no download), scaled to [0, 1]; stratified 80/20 split with random_state=0: 1,437 training and 360 test images.
steps: Load and split: X = (X / 16.0).astype(float32); train_test_split(test_size=0.2, stratify=y, random_state=0); torch.manual_seed(0); print the shapes (1437, 64) (360, 64).

PCA baseline: sklearn PCA with 2 and 8 components fitted on the training set; reconstruct the test set with inverse_transform(transform(X)); print the test MSE per pixel: about 0.0532 (2 components) and 0.0246 (8).

Undercomplete autoencoder: encoder Linear(64, 128)-GELU-Linear(128, d_z), decoder Linear(d_z, 128)-GELU-Linear(128, 64)-sigmoid; MSE loss; a shared train() helper (Adam lr 1e-3, batch 64, 200 epochs, shuffling with a seeded torch.Generator); d_z = 2 and 8; print the test MSE per pixel: about 0.037 and 0.011, below PCA at both sizes; about 7 s per model.

VAE: the source's class with the decoder output used as Bernoulli logits (binary_cross_entropy_with_logits summed over pixels, averaged over the batch), the closed-form KL kept per dimension, and a beta attribute multiplying the KL; d_z = 2, beta = 1, same optimiser and epochs. Print on the test set -ELBO, reconstruction, KL and KL per dimension: about 24.9 = 22.6 + 2.3 nats, per dimension about (1.1, 1.2).

Latent space: scatter the test-set means mu(x) coloured by digit and save the figure; print the 5-nearest-neighbour accuracy of a classifier fitted on training-set codes and scored on test-set codes: PCA-2 0.617, AE-2 0.839, VAE-2 0.750 (raw 64 pixels: 0.978, for reference). Decode a 10 x 10 grid of z on [-2.5, 2.5]^2 from the VAE and a grid over the bounding box of the AE's training codes; save both.
Samples and interpolation: decode 16 draws of z ~ N(0, I), and an 8-step linear interpolation between the latent means of one test '1' and one test '7'; save the figures.

Posterior collapse on purpose: train the d_z = 8 VAE with beta = 0.5, 1 and 4; print total KL, KL per dimension, reconstruction and active units (dimensions with variance of mu_j(x) over the test set above 0.01): beta 0.5 -> KL about 6.5, 8 active; beta 1 -> about 3.6, 6 active; beta 4 -> 0.00, 0 active, reconstruction about 27.2 nats against 21.0 at beta 1. Then train beta = 1 with the source's MSE-sum loss (implied sigma_x^2 = 1/2): KL about 0.6, 3 active.

Anomaly detector: train the d_z = 8 autoencoder on training digits 0-8 only, with 20% of them held out (random_state=0) for validation; threshold = 95th percentile of the validation errors (about 0.026 per pixel); print the false-alarm rate on test digits 0-8 (about 0.04), the detection rate on test 9s (about 0.58) and ROC AUC (about 0.95); repeat with PCA (8 components) reconstruction error, the classical Q statistic: AUC about 0.79, detection about 0.22 at a false-alarm rate of about 0.08.
expected_observations: The autoencoder beats PCA at equal code size (0.037 against 0.053 at d_z = 2) because digits lie on a curved manifold; at d_z = 8 the gap is more than twofold.

The VAE's 2D codes overlap more than the plain autoencoder's (5-NN accuracy 0.75 against 0.84) because the KL term pulls every code toward N(0, I); in exchange every point of the VAE's grid decodes to a plausible digit, while the autoencoder's grid has implausible regions between clusters.

The KL weight controls collapse: at beta = 4 every dimension has KL 0.00, the decoder ignores z and outputs an average digit. The source's MSE-sum loss acts like a weak reconstruction term (sigma_x^2 = 1/2) and leaves only 3 of 8 dimensions active.

An AUC of 0.95 does not mean 95% detection: at a threshold that gives about 5% false alarms only about 58% of 9s are caught, because many 9s resemble digits the model reconstructs well. The PCA baseline is clearly worse, which is the comparison that justifies the network.
extensions: KL warm-up: ramp beta linearly from 0 to 1 over the first 50 epochs; active units rise from 6 to 8 (the two extra carry little KL). Ramp to beta = 4 instead and the model still collapses: warm-up fixes collapse caused by the optimisation path, not collapse that is the optimum of the objective.

Source exercise 2: train the VAE with d_x = 2 and d_z = 2 on 3,000 points from three 2D Gaussian clusters (means (-2, 0), (2, 0), (0, 2.5), standard deviation 0.3) with a Gaussian decoder, and plot the latent means coloured by cluster; then set d_z = 1 and see whether the clusters stay apart.

Change the anomalous digit: holding out 8 gives detection about 0.83 (AUC 0.96) and holding out 0 about 1.00 (AUC 0.999) at the same false-alarm setting; explain which digits are hard anomalies and why.

labs.title: A diffusion model on two moons, with classifier-free guidance
labs.goal: Implement the DDPM forward process, train a noise-prediction network on 2D data, sample with the reverse process and with DDIM, and measure what classifier-free guidance and the number of steps do to fidelity and diversity.
labs.data: Synthetic: sklearn make_moons(n_samples=10000, noise=0.05, random_state=0), standardised with its own mean and standard deviation; a reference set make_moons(5000, noise=0.05, random_state=1) on the same scale for evaluation; the moon label is the condition.
steps: Schedule: cosine (s = 0.008) with T = 200 and beta_t = min(1 - alpha-bar_t/alpha-bar_{t-1}, 0.5); print alpha-bar_1 (about 0.99975), alpha-bar_100 (about 0.494), alpha-bar_200 (about 6.8e-5) and the last three uncapped betas (0.5555, 0.75, 1.0) to show why the cap is there; plot alpha-bar_t.
Forward process: one fixed noise draw per point; scatter x_t = sqrt(alpha-bar_t) x_0 + sqrt(1 - alpha-bar_t) eps at t = 0, 50, 100, 150, 175 and 200 (figure).

Model: an MLP eps_theta(x_t, t, c) whose input is x_t (2 numbers) concatenated with [32-dimensional sinusoidal embedding of t plus a learned 32-dimensional embedding of c in {0, 1, 2 = null}]; three hidden layers of 128 with SiLU; output 2. Print the parameter count, 37,858.

Training: QUICK = False runs 20,000 steps, QUICK = True 8,000; batches of 512 from the 10,000 points; t uniform on {1..200}; the condition replaced by null with probability 0.2; loss = MSE between eps and eps_theta; Adam lr 1e-3 with cosine decay to 0. Print the loss at every 20% of training (noisy, settling between about 0.28 and 0.34). The full run takes about 0.5-2 minutes on a laptop CPU.

Ancestral sampling (Ho et al.'s Algorithm 2) with the null condition: 2,000 samples, recording x_t before the update at t = 200, 150, 100, 50, 20 and 5, and the final x_0 (figure). Print mean nearest-neighbour distances: samples to reference (precision-like) about 0.020, against 0.013 for fresh data and 0.242 for N(0, I) draws; reference to samples (recall-like) about 0.021, against 0.021 for fresh data and 0.051 for noise; and the precision-like distance at each snapshot (about 0.246, 0.234, 0.211, 0.134, 0.056, 0.025). With QUICK = True expect precision about 0.04 and recall about 0.027.

Classifier-free guidance: 1,000 samples of class 0 with eps-tilde = eps_theta(x_t, t, null) + w (eps_theta(x_t, t, 0) - eps_theta(x_t, t, null)) for w = 0, 1, 3, 7; a 15-NN classifier fitted on the reference set labels each sample. Print the fraction in class 0 (about 0.50, 1.00, 1.00, 1.00), the precision-like distance (about 0.021, 0.014, 0.013, 0.033) and the recall-like distance to the class-0 reference points (about 0.032, 0.022, 0.029, 0.046); figure with four panels.

DDIM: the deterministic update x-hat_0 = (x_t - sqrt(1 - alpha-bar_t) eps_theta)/sqrt(alpha-bar_t), x_{t'} = sqrt(alpha-bar_{t'}) x-hat_0 + sqrt(1 - alpha-bar_{t'}) eps_theta, on K evenly spaced steps from 200 to 0, unconditional, K = 200, 50, 20, 10, 5, 2, 1. Print the precision- and recall-like distances (about 0.023/0.023, 0.025/0.024, 0.030/0.027, 0.037/0.035, 0.045/0.045, 0.10/0.08, 1.57/0.07) and the sampling time for each K.
expected_observations: Structure appears late in the reverse process: samples are indistinguishable from noise until about t = 50, and most of the precision is gained in the last 20 steps.
The unconditional samples are almost as close to the data as fresh data are (0.020 against 0.013) and cover both moons (recall 0.021 against 0.021).

Guidance trades diversity for fidelity: w = 1 already puts every sample on the requested moon; w = 3 and 7 squeeze the samples toward the densest part of the moon (the recall distance doubles by w = 7), and at w = 7 precision starts to worsen as samples overshoot.

DDIM with 20-50 steps is close to the 200-step ancestral sampler; below about 10 steps quality falls quickly, and a single step returns a scaled-up posterior mean far from the data: the cost of diffusion is its number of steps.

With the uncapped cosine schedule (beta_T = 0.999) the first reverse step multiplies errors by 31.6; in a prototype run this made the w = 7 samples diverge (precision distance 1.34). The cap at 0.5 keeps the factor at 1.41.
extensions: Restore the cap to 0.999 and repeat the guidance step; then keep the 0.999 cap but compute x-hat_0, clip it to [-3, 3] and use the posterior-mean update instead.

Train the non-saturating GAN of Section 4 (generator and discriminator: MLPs with three hidden layers of 128, Adam lr 1e-3, betas (0.5, 0.999)) on the same standardised moons for 6,000 steps and compare its precision and recall distances with the diffusion model's; note it needs one forward pass per sample.

Replace the schedule by Ho et al.'s linear range at T = 200 (alpha-bar_T = 0.13) and compare; on these standardised 2D data the damage is small (a prototype run gave precision 0.021 and recall 0.022). Explain why 2D standardised data hide a problem that matters for images.

labs.title: A graph convolutional network from scratch: single points of failure in fault trees
labs.goal: Build the normalised adjacency and message passing by hand, train GCNs of increasing depth to find single points of failure in synthetic fault trees, compare them with honest baselines, and see over-smoothing and the value of direction-aware messages.
labs.data: Synthetic: a fault-tree generator written in the lab (300 trees from numpy default_rng(0); 200 for training and 100 for testing, split by tree), plus the 12-node cooling-system tree of Section 8 built by hand. No graph library is needed.
steps: Generator: the top event is a gate (OR with probability 0.6, else AND); every gate has 2-4 inputs, uniformly; an input is a gate with probability 0.6 at depths 0-1 and 0.35 at depth 2, never below depth 3, otherwise a basic event. Features: one-hot [OR, AND, BASIC] plus a TOP flag (4 numbers). Label for each basic event: 1 if every gate on its path to the top is OR (a single point of failure), else 0; gates are not scored. Print: about 28.1 nodes per tree (3 to 95); 5,536 training and 2,903 test nodes; 3,740 training basic events (22.0% single points of failure) and 1,971 test basic events (16.2%); test basic events by depth {1: 124, 2: 213, 3: 583, 4: 1051}.
Check the labeller on the hand-built cooling-system tree: it must return E1, E5 and E6.

Baselines on the test basic events: majority class (never a single point of failure) 0.838; 'the event's own gate is OR' 0.551, a plausible rule that is worse than the majority class because most such events have an AND gate higher up.

Normalised adjacency as an edge list: both edge directions plus self-loops, weights 1/sqrt(d-tilde_i d-tilde_j); propagate(H) = torch.zeros_like(H).index_add_(0, i, w[:, None] * H[j]). Verify on the 12-node tree against the dense D-tilde^{-1/2}(A + I)D-tilde^{-1/2} @ H: maximum absolute difference about 1e-7.

GCN: Linear(4, 32) input layer, L layers of H <- ReLU(A-hat H W), Linear(32, 2) output; full-batch Adam lr 1e-2, weight decay 5e-4, 200 epochs, cross-entropy on the training basic events only; L = 1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 16. Print test accuracy and accuracy by depth: about 0.88, 0.88-0.89, 0.91, 0.94-0.96, 0.838, 0.838 (values in the 0.9s move by a point or two with thread count and PyTorch version).

Over-smoothing without training: on the largest test tree (72 nodes) print the mean pairwise cosine similarity of the rows of A-hat^k X for k = 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 (about 0.82, 0.88, 0.91, 0.94, 0.96, 0.98, 0.99). Then train L = 16 with residual updates H <- H + ReLU(A-hat H W): about 0.95-0.97.

Direction-aware layer: H <- ReLU(W_s H + (message from the node's gate) W_p + (mean of the messages from its inputs) W_c), two index_add_ calls on the directed edge list; L = 2, 3, 4: about 0.916, 0.963, 1.000, with accuracy 1.0 at every depth up to L.

Apply the L = 4 direction-aware model to the 12-node cooling-system tree and print the predicted single points of failure: E1, E5 and E6 (a prototype run also found the undirected L = 4 GCN correct on this small tree).
expected_observations: Accuracy by depth shows the receptive field: an L-layer model is reliable only for events at most L hops below the top; the direction-aware model makes this exact.

The undirected GCN improves up to about 4 layers; the plain 8- and 16-layer models then predict the majority class for every event. Their node features are nearly identical (the untrained A-hat^k X similarity climbs toward 1), and with no residual path a deep stack also trains poorly; residual connections restore it.

A symmetric adjacency gives each event a mixture of its gate, its siblings and, two hops away, their gate's other inputs; the property depends only on the gates above. Separate parent and child weights let the network compute 'every gate above is OR' exactly.
The rule that sounds right ('its gate is OR', 0.551) is worse than the majority class (0.838); every model must be compared with both.
extensions: Split by node instead of by tree (a random 70/30 split over all nodes of all 300 trees) and compare; explain why per-node splits flatter a model that will be used on new trees.
Add each node's depth as a fifth feature and retrain the undirected GCN with L = 4; does it close the gap to the direction-aware model?
The source's question, best tried after exercise e9: train a 2-layer GCN to predict whether a node is a basic event, and compare it with the baseline you named in e9. What has the GCN learned?

labs.title: A physics-informed network for a damped oscillator: forward, failure, fixes and an inverse problem
labs.goal: Train a PINN on an ODE with a known exact solution, reproduce the trivial-solution failure, fix it three ways, and recover an unknown damping ratio from twelve noisy readings, comparing with a classical fit.
labs.data: Synthetic: the exact solution of u'' + 2 zeta w0 u' + w0^2 u = 0 with w0 = 2 pi rad/s, zeta = 0.1, u(0) = 1, u'(0) = 0 on t in [0, 2] s; 12 'measurements' at random times (torch.Generator seed 1) with Gaussian noise of standard deviation 0.02.
steps: Set-up: torch.manual_seed(0); torch.set_num_threads(1), because a network this small gains nothing from more threads (about 1.2 ms per training step with one thread or four in a prototype) and one thread avoids large slowdowns when other programs compete for the cores (a prototype run slowed from about 1.2 to 30 ms per step under such contention); exact(t) = exp(-zeta w0 t)(cos(wd t) + (zeta w0/wd) sin(wd t)); 1,000 test times; a relative L2 error helper; plot the exact solution.

Network and derivatives: u_theta(t) an MLP 1 -> 32 -> 32 -> 32 -> 1 with tanh and the input divided by t_end; d(u, t) = torch.autograd.grad(u, t, torch.ones_like(u), create_graph=True)[0]; 200 evenly spaced collocation points with requires_grad; loss = mean residual^2 + lambda_ic[(u(0) - 1)^2 + u'(0)^2]; Adam lr 1e-3.

Dimensional residual u'' + 2 zeta w0 u' + w0^2 u, lambda_ic = 1, 3,000 steps: print both loss terms at step 0 (residual about 52.5, initial conditions about 1.36) and at the end; final residual about 6e-3 and initial-condition term about 0.99; relative L2 error about 0.999 and max |u| about 0.006, the trivial solution.
lambda_ic = 0, 3,000 steps: residual about 5e-6, max |u| about 1e-4, error 1.000; zero satisfies the equation exactly.
lambda_ic = 100, 10,000 steps: error about 0.015 at 5,000 steps and 0.004 at 10,000.

Non-dimensional: t-hat = w0 t on [0, 4 pi], residual u'' + 2 zeta u' + u with derivatives in t-hat, lambda_ic = 1, 10,000 steps: residual at step 0 about 0.034; error about 0.06 at 5,000, 0.008 at 7,500 and 0.0004 at 10,000 steps.

Inverse problem: zeta unknown, parameterised as log zeta from a starting value of 0.5 and optimised with the network; loss = non-dimensional residual + initial conditions + 10 x mean squared error on the 12 readings; 10,000 steps. Print zeta every 1,000 steps (about 0.42, 0.24, 0.17, ..., 0.12 at 5,000 and 0.0987 at 10,000) and the solution's error (about 0.02).
Classical baseline: scipy.optimize.curve_fit of the closed-form solution to the same 12 readings: zeta about 0.0977 +/- 0.0015.
expected_observations: In dimensional units the residual term starts about 40 times larger than the initial-condition term, and the optimiser drives the network to zero, which satisfies the equation: the loss is small and the answer is wrong.
Weighting the initial conditions fixes it; non-dimensionalising fixes it better, because the equation's terms become of order 1 and the loss terms comparable without hand-tuned weights.

The inverse problem recovers zeta to within a few per cent from 12 noisy readings, as a least-squares fit of the closed form does: when a closed form exists, use it; the PINN earns its cost when it does not.

Second derivatives through autograd cost several forward passes each, yet a network this small trains 10,000 steps in about 15 s on a desktop CPU (well under a minute on a laptop); the whole lab runs in about one to three minutes.
extensions: Hard constraint: use u = 1 + (t/t_end)^2 N_theta(t), drop the initial-condition term and train in dimensional units for 10,000 steps: no trivial solution is possible, yet the error is still about 0.09 because the scaling problem remains.
Spectral bias: set w0 = 8 pi (eight periods in 2 s) in the non-dimensional form and train again; then feed Fourier features [sin(k t-hat), cos(k t-hat)] for k = 1, 2, 4 as extra inputs and compare.
Exercise e12 starts from this code and moves to the heat equation.

labs.title: Contrastive pretraining on unlabelled vibration signals
labs.goal: Pretrain an encoder with InfoNCE on unlabelled machine-vibration windows, measure with a linear probe how much it helps when only a few faults are labelled, compare it with raw and spectral features, and show that the augmentations decide what is learned.
labs.data: Synthetic, generated in the lab with numpy default_rng(0): 1-second windows sampled at 256 Hz, four classes; 4,000 windows for pretraining (labels kept aside for probing) and 2,000 test windows.
steps: Generator: shaft speed f_r uniform on 9-11 Hz; healthy = 1.0 sin(2 pi f_r t + phi_1) + 0.2 sin(2 pi 2 f_r t + phi_2); imbalance: 1x amplitude 2.5; misalignment: 1x, 2x and 3x amplitudes 1.0, 1.5 and 0.5; bearing defect: healthy plus impulses repeating at 3.57 f_r, each a 60 Hz oscillation of amplitude 1.5 decaying at 30 per second; random phases; sensor gain uniform on 0.8-1.2; additive noise of standard deviation 0.3. Plot one window per class and its magnitude spectrum.

Probe protocol: StandardScaler + LogisticRegression(max_iter=5000) fitted on 5, 20 or 100 labelled windows per class drawn from the pretraining pool (5 random draws, averaged), scored on the 2,000 test windows.
Baselines: raw waveform about 0.376 / 0.447 / 0.485 (5 / 20 / 100 labels per class); FFT magnitude (129 bins) about 0.790 / 0.890 / 0.975; an untrained encoder's h about 0.494 / 0.733 / 0.882.

Loss: nt_xent(z1, z2, tau) = cross-entropy over the 2B x 2B cosine-similarity matrix (B the batch) divided by tau, with the diagonal set to -infinity and the twin view as target. Sanity check: F.cross_entropy(torch.tensor([[0.9, 0.2, 0.1, -0.3]]) / tau, torch.tensor([0])) gives 0.810 for tau = 1 and 0.0013 for tau = 0.1 (Section 11's worked example).

Pretraining: encoder MLP 256 -> 256 -> 128 (h) and projection head ReLU -> 64 (z, L2-normalised); augmentations: random circular time shift, gain log-uniform on 0.8-1.25, added noise of standard deviation 0.1; tau = 0.2, batch B = 256 (510 negatives per view), Adam lr 1e-3, 60 epochs (900 steps, about 8 s). Print the final loss (about 2.39) against log(2B - 1) = log 511 = 6.24, the loss of collapsed embeddings.
Probe h: about 0.929 / 0.989 / 0.996; probe z: about 0.609 / 0.919 / 0.998. Repeat pretraining with seeds 1 and 2: 5-label accuracy about 0.926 and 0.919.

Ablation: pretrain without the time shift (gain and noise only): about 0.576 / 0.865 / 0.973; with no augmentation: about 0.540 / 0.803 / 0.951. Print the 100-label confusion matrix of the no-shift model: misalignment mistaken for imbalance (about 36 of 482) and bearing defects for healthy (about 18 of 518).
expected_observations: A linear classifier on the raw waveform is near chance: with random phases no fixed linear combination of samples identifies a class. Spectral magnitudes, the classical engineering feature, remove phase by construction and do well once there are enough labels.

Contrastive pretraining with a time-shift augmentation learns a phase-invariant representation without labels: with 5 labels per class it beats the FFT features by about 14 points; with 100 they are within 2 points.
The augmentation is the supervision: without the time shift the learned features are barely better than an untrained encoder's.
The projection head absorbs what the augmentations vary; probing z with few labels is far worse than probing h, which is why SimCLR keeps h.
The InfoNCE loss stays well above zero (about 2.39) but far below log(2B - 1) = 6.24, the value for embeddings that carry no information.
extensions: Widen the gain augmentation to 0.25-4: the probe barely changes (about 0.952 / 0.993 / 0.997), because healthy and imbalance windows also differ in harmonic ratios and signal-to-noise ratio. Design an augmentation that does destroy a class distinction in these data and confirm it with the confusion matrix.
Vary tau over 0.05, 0.5 and 1.0 (5-label accuracy about 0.90, 0.95 and 0.95 in a prototype run) and the batch size over 64 and 512.
Add a fifth class to the test set only (mechanical looseness: many harmonics of f_r with decaying amplitudes) and check whether the pretrained h separates it in a 2D PCA plot without retraining.

exercises.prompt: An autoencoder maps 64-pixel images to a 128-dimensional code and back, with no other constraint, and its training reconstruction error reaches zero. Explain why the code is useless as a representation, and name two changes that would force the network to learn the structure of the data.
exercises.solution_sketch: With d_z >= d_x the network can learn the identity (or any invertible map) and reconstruct perfectly without capturing which inputs are likely. Fixes: a bottleneck d_z < d_x; a denoising objective (corrupt or mask the input, reconstruct the clean one), which forces it to map points back to the data; a sparsity penalty on z; or a VAE's KL term, which limits the information z can carry.

exercises.prompt: (a) Starting from log p_theta(x) = log of the integral of p_theta(x|z) p(z) dz, insert q_phi(z|x)/q_phi(z|x), apply Jensen's inequality and obtain the ELBO E_q[log p_theta(x|z)] - D_KL(q_phi(z|x) || p(z)). (b) Without Jensen, show that log p_theta(x) - ELBO = D_KL(q_phi(z|x) || p_theta(z|x)), and say when the bound is tight. (c) Show that D_KL(N(mu, sigma^2) || N(0, 1)) = (1/2)(mu^2 + sigma^2 - log sigma^2 - 1) and that for a diagonal Gaussian the KL is a sum over dimensions; evaluate it for mu = (0.3, -1.5, 0.0), sigma = (0.8, 1.0, 2.0), and say what each dimension pays for.
exercises.solution_sketch: (a) log p(x) = log E_q[p(x|z)p(z)/q(z|x)] >= E_q[log p(x|z) + log p(z) - log q(z|x)] = E_q[log p(x|z)] - D_KL(q || p(z)), since log is concave. (b) For any z, p(x) = p(x|z)p(z)/p(z|x); take logs and the expectation under q: log p(x) = E_q[log(p(x|z)p(z)/q)] + E_q[log(q/p(z|x))] = ELBO + D_KL(q || p(z|x)) >= ELBO, tight exactly when q(z|x) = p_theta(z|x). (c) D_KL = E_q[log q - log p] = E_q[-(1/2)log sigma^2 - (z - mu)^2/(2 sigma^2) + z^2/2] = -(1/2)log sigma^2 - 1/2 + (1/2)(mu^2 + sigma^2); independent dimensions have additive log densities, so the KLs add. Numbers: (1/2)(0.09 + 0.64 + 0.4463 - 1) = 0.0881, (1/2)(2.25 + 1 - 0 - 1) = 1.125 and (1/2)(0 + 4 - 1.3863 - 1) = 0.8069, total 2.020 nats. The second dimension pays only for its mean, the third only for its width (a posterior wider than the prior costs too), the first a little for both.

exercises.prompt: A VAE with d_z = 8 reports these per-dimension KL values on the test set, in nats: (2.1, 1.7, 0.003, 0.002, 1.2, 0.001, 0.004, 0.002). How many latent dimensions carry information about x? What does the decoder do with the rest? Name two changes you would try if the task needs more of them.
exercises.solution_sketch: Three (dimensions 1, 2 and 5). In the others q(z_j|x) is essentially N(0, 1) for every x, so z_j is noise independent of the input and the decoder learns to ignore it: partial posterior collapse. Fixes: lower the KL weight (beta < 1) or warm it up from 0; free bits; a likelihood that weights reconstruction properly (Bernoulli for [0, 1] pixels, or a smaller decoder variance than the sigma_x^2 = 1/2 implied by an MSE-sum loss); a less powerful decoder.

exercises.prompt: (a) For fixed G, the GAN value is V = integral of [p_data(x) log D(x) + p_g(x) log(1 - D(x))] dx. Maximise the integrand pointwise to obtain D*(x). (b) Substitute D* and show that V(G, D*) = -log 4 + 2 JSD(p_data || p_g), where JSD(p || q) = (1/2)KL(p || m) + (1/2)KL(q || m) and m = (p + q)/2. (c) Check your result on three points: p_data = (0.6, 0.3, 0.1), p_g = (0.2, 0.3, 0.5).

A GAN trained on cross-section images of turbine blades produces samples an engineer cannot tell from real ones, and its discriminator's accuracy hovers around 50%. Describe one measurement that would reveal mode collapse: what you compute, what you compare it with, and what result would indicate collapse. Then explain why the discriminator's 50% accuracy is no evidence against it.
exercises.solution_sketch: Measure coverage, not realism. Embed held-out real sections and an equal number of generated ones in a feature space (or describe each by a vector of geometric parameters); for each held-out real section compute the distance to its nearest generated sample (recall-like), and compare with the same distance computed to an equally large set of other real sections. Collapse shows as a recall-like distance well above that real-to-real reference, concentrated in some kinds of section, or as clusters of the real data with no samples near them; the precision-like distance, samples to data, stays small, which is why realism cannot reveal it. Distances from samples to the training set also flag near-copies. The 50% accuracy says only that D cannot separate samples from data where the samples fall: regions of p_data the generator never visits contribute nothing to the loss G sees, and a cycling discriminator can sit near 50% while G hops between a few modes.

exercises.prompt: Show that the per-step forward process q(x_t | x_{t-1}) = N(sqrt(1 - beta_t) x_{t-1}, beta_t I) gives q(x_t | x_0) = N(sqrt(alpha-bar_t) x_0, (1 - alpha-bar_t) I) with alpha-bar_t = product over s <= t of (1 - beta_s). Write x_t = sqrt(alpha_t) x_{t-1} + sqrt(1 - alpha_t) eps_t, assume the result for t - 1, and use the fact that a sum of independent zero-mean Gaussians is Gaussian with the sum of the variances.
exercises.solution_sketch: Base case t = 1: x_1 = sqrt(alpha_1) x_0 + sqrt(1 - alpha_1) eps_1, mean sqrt(alpha-bar_1) x_0, variance 1 - alpha-bar_1. Step: if x_{t-1} = sqrt(alpha-bar_{t-1}) x_0 + sqrt(1 - alpha-bar_{t-1}) eps-bar, then x_t = sqrt(alpha_t alpha-bar_{t-1}) x_0 + sqrt(alpha_t) sqrt(1 - alpha-bar_{t-1}) eps-bar + sqrt(1 - alpha_t) eps_t. The two noise terms are independent with variances alpha_t (1 - alpha-bar_{t-1}) and 1 - alpha_t, summing to 1 - alpha_t alpha-bar_{t-1} = 1 - alpha-bar_t; the mean is sqrt(alpha-bar_t) x_0. So x_t = sqrt(alpha-bar_t) x_0 + sqrt(1 - alpha-bar_t) eps with a single eps ~ N(0, I).

exercises.prompt: Ho et al.'s linear schedule runs beta_t evenly from 1e-4 to 0.02 over T = 1000 steps. (a) Estimate alpha-bar_T using log(1 - beta) approx -beta and compare with the exact product, 4.04e-5. (b) Someone keeps the same beta range but sets T = 100. Estimate alpha-bar_T and sqrt(alpha-bar_T). (c) Explain what goes wrong when that model is sampled from x_T ~ N(0, I), and give two fixes.
exercises.solution_sketch: (a) sum of beta_t = 1000 x 0.01005 = 10.05, so alpha-bar_T approx e^-10.05 = 4.3e-5, close to the exact 4.04e-5 (the second-order term -sum beta^2/2 accounts for most of the difference). (b) sum = 100 x 0.01005 = 1.005, alpha-bar_T approx e^-1.005 = 0.366 (exact 0.364), sqrt(alpha-bar_T) approx 0.60: at the noisiest step 60% of the signal amplitude remains. (c) The network never saw pure noise at t = T, but sampling starts from it: a train-test mismatch at the first step that propagates (on images, models trained this way cannot produce very bright or very dark images, Lin et al. 2024). Fixes: rescale beta so that alpha-bar_T is near 0 (for example scale the range by 1000/T), use the cosine schedule, or rescale the schedule to zero terminal SNR.

exercises.prompt: A gate with three basic-event inputs forms a star graph: centre c joined to leaves a, b and d. (a) Write A-hat = D-tilde^{-1/2}(A + I)D-tilde^{-1/2}. (b) With the scalar feature x = (1, 0, 0, 0) (centre first), compute A-hat x and A-hat^2 x. (c) Find the limit of A-hat^k x as k grows, using the eigenvector u proportional to D-tilde^{1/2} 1, and the ratio of the centre's value to a leaf's. (d) The eigenvalues of A-hat are 1, 0.5, 0.5 and -0.25, and the eigenvectors for 0.5 are zero at the centre and sum to zero over the leaves. How fast does A-hat^k x approach its limit for this x, and why not as 0.5^k?
exercises.solution_sketch: (a) d-tilde = (4, 2, 2, 2): A-hat_cc = 1/4, A-hat_c,leaf = 1/sqrt(8) = 0.3536, A-hat_leaf,leaf = 1/2, zero between leaves. (b) A-hat x = (0.25, 0.3536, 0.3536, 0.3536); A-hat^2 x = (0.25 x 0.25 + 3 x 0.3536^2, 0.3536 x 0.25 + 0.5 x 0.3536, ...) = (0.4375, 0.2652, 0.2652, 0.2652). (c) u = (2, sqrt 2, sqrt 2, sqrt 2)/sqrt 10 = (0.6325, 0.4472, 0.4472, 0.4472); the limit is u (u^T x) = 0.6325 u = (0.4, 0.2828, 0.2828, 0.2828), ratio sqrt(d-tilde_c/d-tilde_leaf) = sqrt 2. (d) x takes the same value (0) on every leaf, so it has no component along the two lambda = 0.5 eigenvectors. What separates it from its limit, x - u(u^T x) = (0.6, -0.2828, -0.2828, -0.2828), lies entirely along the lambda = -0.25 eigenvector (proportional to (-2.121, 1, 1, 1)), so the error shrinks by a factor of 4 at every step and flips sign: relative errors ||A-hat^k x - limit|| / ||limit|| of 0.306, 0.0765, 0.0191 and 0.0048 for k = 1 to 4, below 1% from k = 4. The second-largest |lambda| bounds the rate for general features; the actual rate is set by the eigenvectors the features touch. A leaf's feature, x = (0, 1, 0, 0), does have a lambda = 0.5 component and converges as 0.5^k: relative error 0.935 at k = 1, 0.114 at k = 4 and 0.0071 at k = 8, below 1% only from k = 8.

exercises.prompt: A colleague trains a two-layer GCN to predict which nodes of fault trees are basic events, with node degree among the features, and reports 99% test accuracy. What baseline should the result be compared with, what does that baseline score, and what task would actually test whether a GNN has learned something about fault-tree structure?
exercises.solution_sketch: In a fault tree the basic events are exactly the leaves: every non-top node with one neighbour is a basic event, and every gate has at least two inputs. The leaf rule scores 100%, so the GCN has learned nothing the structure did not give for free, and does slightly worse. A meaningful task needs information several hops away, such as single points of failure (every gate on the path to the top is OR; Lab 3), evaluated with a split by tree, not by node.

exercises.prompt: Graph P is the complete bipartite graph K_{3,3}: two rows of three nodes, each node joined to all three nodes of the other row. Graph Q is the triangular prism: two triangles with corresponding corners joined. Every node has the same feature vector. Explain why any message-passing GNN (GCN, GAT, GIN) gives every node the same embedding in both graphs, whatever the number of layers, and why a sum or mean readout cannot tell P from Q. Propose one input feature that would.
exercises.solution_sketch: Both graphs have 6 nodes and 9 edges, and every node has exactly three neighbours. With identical initial features every node receives three identical messages at the first layer and computes the same update, and by induction all twelve nodes stay identical at every layer: GCN's weights are all 1/sqrt(4 x 4) = 1/4, GAT's attention is uniform over identical neighbours, GIN's sum is the same everywhere. A sum or mean over six identical node vectors is then the same for P and Q. This is the 1-Weisfeiler-Lehman limit: colour refinement never splits the nodes of a regular graph, and message passing is bounded by that test. Yet the graphs differ, since the prism contains two triangles and K_{3,3}, being bipartite, none. Features that break the tie: the number of triangles through each node (1 in Q, 0 in P), the length of the shortest cycle through it (3 against 4), random node identifiers, or a spectral positional encoding (the adjacency eigenvalues are 3, 0, 0, 0, 0, -3 for P and 3, 1, 0, 0, -2, -2 for Q).

exercises.prompt: For u'' + 2 zeta w0 u' + w0^2 u = 0 with u(0) = 1, u'(0) = 0, a student proposes the trial solution u(t) = exp(-zeta w0 t) cos(w0 t): decaying, but at the undamped frequency. (a) Compute the residual r(t) symbolically. (b) Evaluate r(0) and the initial-condition terms (u(0) - 1)^2 and u'(0)^2 for zeta = 0.1 and w0 = 2 pi. (c) What two changes give the exact solution, and how would a PINN's loss report the trial function's error?
exercises.solution_sketch: (a) With a = zeta w0: u' = -exp(-at)(a cos(w0 t) + w0 sin(w0 t)), u'' = exp(-at)((a^2 - w0^2) cos(w0 t) + 2 a w0 sin(w0 t)); substituting, the sine terms cancel and r(t) = -zeta^2 w0^2 exp(-zeta w0 t) cos(w0 t). (b) r(0) = -zeta^2 w0^2 = -0.395; (u(0) - 1)^2 = 0; u'(0) = -zeta w0 = -0.628, so u'(0)^2 = 0.395. (c) Use the damped frequency wd = w0 sqrt(1 - zeta^2) and add (zeta w0/wd) sin(wd t) so that u'(0) = 0. A PINN's loss would show the error in two terms: a residual that starts at r(0) = -0.39 and decays with the envelope, giving a residual loss (the mean of r^2 over [0, 2] s) of about 0.029, and an initial-velocity term u'(0)^2 = 0.39; the initial-position term is 0.

exercises.prompt: Adapt Lab 4's code to the heat equation u_t = u_xx on x in [0, 1], t in [0, 0.2], with u(x, 0) = sin(pi x) and u(0, t) = u(1, t) = 0. Use a tanh MLP (2 -> 32 -> 32 -> 32 -> 1) with inputs (x, t/0.2), 1,000 random collocation points redrawn every step, 100 initial-condition points and 100 points on each boundary, Adam lr 1e-3, 8,000 steps, every loss weight 1, torch.set_num_threads(1). Report the relative L2 error against the exact solution exp(-pi^2 t) sin(pi x) on a 101 x 51 grid. Then remove the boundary term, train again from the same seed, and report the error and the values u(0, 0.2), u(0.5, 0.2) and u(1, 0.2). Explain what the network converged to.
exercises.solution_sketch: With the boundary term the error is about 0.005 after 8,000 steps (a prototype run gave 0.022 at 2,000 steps, 0.012 at 4,000 and 0.0047 at 8,000), and u(0.5, 0.2) is about 0.137 against the exact 0.139; each run takes under a minute on one thread. Without the boundary term the PDE residual is just as small (about 4e-5) and the initial condition is still met, but the answer is wrong: in the prototype the relative error was 0.82, with u(0, 0.2) about -0.71, u(0.5, 0.2) about -0.24 and u(1, 0.2) about -0.73 (the exact digits depend on the seed). On a bounded interval the heat equation with only an initial condition has infinitely many solutions, since heat can flow in or out through the ends, and the network picked one in which the ends cool. A small residual certifies that the equation holds, not that the problem was posed completely.

exercises.prompt: Choose a family for each need and name the first baseline it must beat: (a) a surrogate for the steady temperature field of a finned heat sink across fin heights of 10-30 mm and inlet air speeds of 1-5 m/s, trained on 2,000 CFD runs; (b) the same surrogate is asked about an inlet speed of 12 m/s; (c) 50,000 unlabelled thermal images of weld seams from a production line and 20 labelled defects of four types; (d) a 30-node system architecture model in which some components may be single points of failure.
exercises.solution_sketch: (a) A neural operator, or a mesh-based graph network if each design has its own mesh; the baselines are a Gaussian-process or POD surrogate fitted to the same 2,000 runs, and the CFD solver itself (accuracy, and run time at equal accuracy). (b) 12 m/s lies outside the training family, and the flow may be in a different regime there, so the surrogate's error is unknown: run the solver (or extend the training runs) and state the validity range. (c) Self-supervised pretraining (contrastive or masked) on the unlabelled images, then a linear probe on the 20 labels; the baseline is the same probe, with the same 20 labels, on features that need no pretraining on these images: engineered intensity and texture statistics, or a CNN pretrained on generic images (transfer learning, Module 03). Choose augmentations that keep the temperature pattern, which is the evidence. With no labels at all, an autoencoder trained on good welds would be the anomaly detector. (d) The exact graph algorithm (minimal cut sets) is the baseline and, at this size, the right tool; a direction-aware GNN pays off only when the property cannot be computed exactly or the graphs are many and large.

exercises.prompt: For each case, say whether the augmentation is safe for the downstream task, and why: (a) random 90-degree rotations when pretraining on top-down images of composite plies whose fibre direction (0, +45, -45 or 90 degrees) is to be classified; (b) random resized crops (crop 30-100% of the area, then rescale to the full image size) when pretraining on metallographic micrographs for grain-size estimation; (c) random circular time shifts when pretraining on engine-vibration windows that each start at top dead centre, where faults are told apart by the crank angle at which an impact occurs; (d) added Gaussian noise of standard deviation 0.1, on signals of amplitude about 1, for the same engine windows.
exercises.solution_sketch: (a) Unsafe: a quarter-turn maps 0 degrees to 90 and +45 to -45, so the encoder is taught to treat different classes alike. A half-turn would be safe, because a fibre direction is an axis and is unchanged by 180 degrees. (b) Unsafe: rescaling a crop to full size changes the apparent grain size, which is the quantity to be estimated; crop without rescaling. (c) Unsafe here, although the same augmentation was the essential one in Lab 5: these windows are aligned to the engine cycle, so the timing of the impact within the window is the evidence, and a circular shift destroys it. In Lab 5 the window start was arbitrary. Whether an augmentation is safe depends on the task's evidence, not on the augmentation. (d) Safe in moderation: sensor noise is not evidence, and noise this small leaves the impacts visible; much more noise could bury small impacts, so check per-class probe accuracy.

exercises.prompt: A top-1 mixture-of-experts layer with 8 experts is trained without a load-balancing loss. After 2,000 steps, 71% of tokens go to expert 3 and two experts receive none. Explain the feedback loop that produced this, compute the Switch-style balancing term E sum_e f_e P_e if the mean router probabilities equal the token fractions f = (0.05, 0.08, 0.71, 0.06, 0.05, 0.05, 0, 0), and say what the term's gradient does.
exercises.solution_sketch: An expert that receives more tokens gets more gradient, improves faster, scores higher in the router and receives still more; starved experts never improve (routing collapse). With P = f: sum f_e^2 = 0.0025 + 0.0064 + 0.5041 + 0.0036 + 0.0025 + 0.0025 = 0.5216, times 8 = 4.17, against a minimum of 1.0 at uniform routing. The term is differentiable through P (f is a count), and its gradient lowers the router probability of each expert in proportion to its token load, pushing tokens toward the starved experts.

quiz.question: Which statement about the KL divergence D_KL(q||p) is true?
options: It is symmetric: D_KL(q||p) = D_KL(p||q).
It satisfies the triangle inequality, so it is a distance.
It is bounded above by log 2.
It is non-negative, and zero only when q = p.
quiz.explanation: Jensen's inequality gives D_KL >= 0 with equality iff q = p. It is not symmetric (1.153 against 0.597 nats in Section 1's example) and not a metric; the Jensen-Shannon divergence, not the KL, is bounded by log 2.

quiz.question: In a VAE, log p_theta(x) - ELBO equals:
options: the reconstruction error
D_KL(q_phi(z|x) || p(z))
D_KL(q_phi(z|x) || p_theta(z|x))
zero whenever the decoder is Gaussian
quiz.explanation: The identity log p(x) = ELBO + D_KL(q || p(z|x)) makes the gap the KL to the true posterior. D_KL(q || p(z)) is a term inside the ELBO, not the gap; the reconstruction term is the other ELBO term; the gap is zero only when q equals the posterior, whatever the decoder.

quiz.question: Why does a VAE need the reparameterisation trick?
options: Because drawing z ~ N(mu, sigma^2) is not a differentiable function of mu and sigma; writing z = mu + sigma * eps with eps an input makes it one.
Because the KL divergence between Gaussians has no closed form.
Because the decoder cannot take random inputs.
To force the approximate posterior to equal the prior.
quiz.explanation: Gradients must flow from the reconstruction term back to the encoder through the sample; the reparameterisation moves the randomness into eps. The Gaussian KL does have a closed form; decoders take random inputs at sampling time anyway; forcing q to the prior would be posterior collapse.

quiz.question: Why is the non-saturating generator loss -log D(G(z)) used instead of log(1 - D(G(z)))?
options: It has a different optimum, which prevents mode collapse.
It makes the discriminator train faster.
It turns the Jensen-Shannon divergence into a Wasserstein distance.
Early in training D(G(z)) is near 0, where log(1 - D) has almost no gradient with respect to D's logit, while -log D has a gradient near -1.
quiz.explanation: At D(G(z)) = 0.01 the two logit gradients are -0.01 and -0.99. Both losses share the fixed point p_g = p_data, so the change affects the dynamics, not the optimum; it neither prevents mode collapse nor changes the divergence, and it concerns G's update, not D's.

quiz.question: During DDPM training, how is the noisy input x_t obtained for a randomly drawn t?
options: It must be computed by running the t noising steps from x_0 in sequence.
In one step, x_t = sqrt(alpha-bar_t) x_0 + sqrt(1 - alpha-bar_t) eps.
x_t = x_0 + beta_t eps.
x_t = (1 - alpha-bar_t) x_0 + alpha-bar_t eps.
quiz.explanation: A composition of Gaussian steps is Gaussian, so one draw gives x_t exactly and running the steps is unnecessary. beta_t is the variance of a single step, and the formula with (1 - alpha-bar_t) x_0 swaps signal and noise and uses linear rather than square-root weights.

quiz.question: With classifier-free guidance eps-tilde = eps_theta(x_t, null) + w [eps_theta(x_t, c) - eps_theta(x_t, null)], which statement is correct?
options: w = 0 gives the conditional model.
Guidance needs a separately trained noisy-image classifier.
w = 1 gives the conditional model; w > 1 increases fidelity to c at the cost of diversity.
Guidance halves the number of network evaluations per step.
quiz.explanation: w = 0 is the unconditional model and w = 1 the conditional one; above 1 the prediction is extrapolated toward c (Lab 2: recall distance 0.022 at w = 1, 0.046 at w = 7). Classifier-free guidance needs no classifier, and it doubles the evaluations per step (conditional and unconditional).

quiz.question: In a GCN with self-loops, what is A-hat_ij for an edge between a node with 3 neighbours and a node with 1 neighbour?
quiz.explanation: Self-loops add 1 to each degree, giving 4 and 2, and A-hat_ij = 1/sqrt(d-tilde_i d-tilde_j). 0.577 forgets the self-loops; 0.25 is the random-walk weight seen from the hub; 1 is the unnormalised adjacency.

quiz.question: Repeatedly applying A-hat = D-tilde^{-1/2}(A + I)D-tilde^{-1/2} to the node features of a connected graph makes them converge to:
options: zero
the original features
one common direction for every node, scaled by sqrt(d-tilde_i)
one-hot vectors of each node's community
quiz.explanation: A-hat has eigenvalue 1 with eigenvector D-tilde^{1/2} 1 and all other eigenvalues below 1 in magnitude, so A-hat^k X tends to u u^T X: every row is the same vector scaled by sqrt(d-tilde_i). Nothing goes to zero, the original features are lost, and community structure is washed out, not sharpened.

quiz.question: A PINN for u'' + w^2 u = 0 with u(0) = 1, u'(0) = 0 converges to u = 0. The most likely cause is:
options: too many collocation points
the initial-condition term is too weak relative to the residual term, and zero satisfies the equation exactly
the tanh activation
a learning rate that is too small
quiz.explanation: Zero has zero residual for a homogeneous equation; only the condition terms exclude it (Lab 4: residual loss 52.5 against 1.36 at the start in dimensional units). More collocation points and tanh are standard; a small learning rate slows training but does not select the trivial solution.

quiz.question: A DeepONet trained on solver runs for one family of boundary conditions is applied to a boundary condition far outside that family. What should you expect?
options: Unknown accuracy: a surrogate is validated only on the distribution it was trained on, so check against the solver.
The same accuracy, because an operator is learned for all input functions.
Exact results, because the trunk network is a basis.
A shape error, because the branch network rejects new inputs.
quiz.explanation: Operator learning approximates the map on the training distribution; outside it the error is unquantified. The trunk's basis is learned from the same data, and the input shape (m sensor values) is unchanged, so the network runs and returns a confident, unvalidated answer.

quiz.question: With InfoNCE over N = 256 candidates, the largest value the lower bound log N - L on mutual information can certify is about:
options: 2.4 nats
5.55 nats
256 nats
unbounded
quiz.explanation: The loss is at least 0, so log N - L <= log 256 = 5.545 nats; certifying more information needs more candidates. 2.4 is a typical loss value rather than a bound, and 256 confuses N with log N.

quiz.question: A layer has 8 experts and routes each token to its top 2. Compared with one dense FFN of the size of a single expert, it has:
options: 2 times the parameters and 8 times the compute
8 times the parameters and 8 times the compute
the same parameters and a quarter of the compute
8 times the parameters and about 2 times the compute per token
quiz.explanation: All 8 experts are stored, but only 2 run for each token, plus a negligible router; that separation of parameters from compute is the point of MoE (Mixtral: 47B total, 13B active).

papers.citation: Ho, J., Jain, A., Abbeel, P. "Denoising diffusion probabilistic models." NeurIPS, 2020.
papers.why: The paper that made diffusion practical: it ties the variational bound to denoising score matching and shows that a simplified noise-prediction loss gives the best samples. Sections 5-6 and Lab 2 follow it closely.
papers.read: Read the background section (forward process, variational bound, the closed form for q(x_t | x_0)), the section relating diffusion models to denoising autoencoders, especially the reverse-process parameterisation and the simplified training objective, Algorithms 1 and 2, and the ablation table in the experiments that compares parameterisations and objectives. Skim the sample-quality results. Skip progressive coding, interpolation and the appendices, except the derivation of the bound if you want the full algebra.
questions: Find the equation for q(x_t | x_0). Which symbol corresponds to this module's alpha-bar_t?
What does the network predict in their best model, and what does the ablation table show for predicting the mean mu-tilde instead, with the true bound and with the simplified objective?
What T and beta schedule do they use? Compute alpha-bar_T and compare it with the value in Section 5.
Map Algorithms 1 and 2 line by line onto Lab 2's training loop and sampler. Where do they differ?
Why, according to the authors, does the simplified objective improve sample quality? Relate their argument to the weights computed in Section 5 (0.50 at t = 1, about 0.01 at t = 100).

papers.citation: Kipf, T. N., Welling, M. "Semi-supervised classification with graph convolutional networks." ICLR, 2017.
papers.why: Short and clear: it derives the GCN layer from spectral graph convolution in two approximations and shows it working with very few labels; its depth experiment anticipates over-smoothing.
papers.read: Read the section on fast approximate convolutions on graphs (the first-order approximation and the renormalisation trick), the two-layer model for semi-supervised node classification with its forward-model equation, the comparison of propagation models in the results, and the appendix on model depth. On a first reading skip the spectral details if graph Laplacians are new to you, the related work and the dataset statistics.
questions: What is the 'renormalisation trick', and which numerical problem does it address?
Write their two-layer forward model and identify each factor in Lab 3's code.
Which propagation model wins in their comparison, and by how much over the first-order model without the renormalisation?
What happens to training and test accuracy as depth grows in the appendix experiment, with and without residual connections? Compare with Lab 3 at 8, 12 and 16 layers.

papers.citation: Raissi, M., Perdikaris, P., Karniadakis, G. E. "Physics-informed neural networks: a deep learning framework for solving forward and inverse problems involving nonlinear partial differential equations." Journal of Computational Physics, 2019.
papers.why: The paper that named the method and set its pattern: a residual computed by automatic differentiation, collocation points, and inverse problems with trainable coefficients. Reading it after Lab 4 lets you judge its claims against failure modes you have reproduced.
papers.read: Read the introduction, the problem set-up, the continuous-time data-driven solution of PDEs with its Burgers' equation example, and the set-up of the continuous-time data-driven discovery problem (the Navier-Stokes example). Skip the discrete-time Runge-Kutta models and the Korteweg-de Vries example.
questions: How many initial and boundary training points and how many collocation points does the Burgers example use, and what error do the authors report?
Write their residual f for Burgers' equation and map it onto the residual function of Lab 4.
In the discovery problem, which coefficients are learned, from how much data, with what noise, and how accurately are they recovered?
Which claims about accuracy or cost would you check against a classical solver before relying on them, and how (Section 9; McGreivy and Hakim 2024)?

widgets.name: diffusion-explorer
widgets.teaching_point: The forward process turns any data distribution into N(0, I) along a path set by the noise schedule, and the cosine schedule keeps structure longer than the linear one; running the process backwards with an exact denoiser recreates the data, badly when the sampler takes too few steps.
controls: select: dataset - 'ring of 8 Gaussians' (default), 'two moons', 'single Gaussian'
slider: timestep t, integer 0-1000, default 500, applied to both panels
button: play/pause - animates t from 0 to 1000 over 5 s, then stops
button: resample noise - new seed for the fixed per-point noise
select: reverse sampler - 'DDPM ancestral, 1000 steps', 'DDIM 50 steps' (default), 'DDIM 10 steps', 'DDIM 3 steps'
button: run reverse - starts both panels from fresh N(0, I) points and animates the reverse process
toggle: show the data components' means as faint crosses (default on)
displays: two side-by-side square scatter plots (canvas, axes -4 to 4), left 'linear schedule' and right 'cosine schedule', showing the same 1,000 points at the same t; they stack vertically below 640 px width
readouts under each panel: t, alpha-bar_t, signal scale sqrt(alpha-bar_t), noise scale sqrt(1 - alpha-bar_t), SNR = 10 log10(alpha-bar_t / (1 - alpha-bar_t)) dB
a shared small line chart of alpha-bar_t against t for both schedules, a vertical marker at the current t and a dotted line at alpha-bar = 0.01
under each panel, a histogram of the points' x-coordinates (40 bins on [-4, 4]) with the standard normal density overlaid
after a reverse run, for each panel: 'precision' = fraction of final points within 3 sigma of the nearest component mean, and 'components hit' = number of components with at least one such point
widgets.defaults: Ring of 8 Gaussians at t = 500: the left (linear, alpha-bar = 0.079) panel is already a round blob while the right (cosine, alpha-bar = 0.494) still shows eight clusters, so the schedule difference is visible before any interaction.
widgets.spec: Data: every dataset is an equal-weight Gaussian mixture with isotropic component standard deviation sigma. Ring: 8 means at 2(cos(2 pi k/8), sin(2 pi k/8)), sigma = 0.1. Two moons: 24 means, (cos th_j, sin th_j) and (1 - cos th_j, 0.5 - sin th_j) for th_j = pi j/11, j = 0..11, then standardised by subtracting (0.5, 0.25) and dividing by (0.8898, 0.4807) per axis; sigma = 0.08. Single Gaussian: mean (1.5, -1.0), sigma = 0.3. Draw N = 1,000 points x_0 per dataset with a seeded PRNG (mulberry32, seed 1; Box-Muller for normals) and one fixed eps_i ~ N(0, I) per point. Schedules with T = 1000: linear beta_t = 1e-4 + (0.02 - 1e-4)(t - 1)/999; cosine alpha-bar_t = f(t)/f(0), f(t) = cos^2(((t/1000) + 0.008)/1.008 * pi/2), beta_t = min(1 - alpha-bar_t/alpha-bar_{t-1}, 0.999); for both alpha-bar_0 = 1 and alpha-bar_t = product of (1 - beta_s); precompute arrays in double precision. Forward: x_t = sqrt(alpha-bar_t) x_0 + sqrt(1 - alpha-bar_t) eps, with no loop, so the slider moves points continuously. Reverse, per panel: start from 1,000 fresh N(0, I) points; the exact posterior mean for the mixture is computed with v_t = alpha-bar_t sigma^2 + 1 - alpha-bar_t, log r_k = -||x_t - sqrt(alpha-bar_t) mu_k||^2 / (2 v_t) normalised by log-sum-exp, m_k = mu_k + (sqrt(alpha-bar_t) sigma^2 / v_t)(x_t - sqrt(alpha-bar_t) mu_k), x-hat_0 = sum_k r_k m_k. DDPM: for t = 1000..1, x_{t-1} = c0 x-hat_0 + c1 x_t + sqrt(beta-tilde_t) z with c0 = sqrt(alpha-bar_{t-1}) beta_t / (1 - alpha-bar_t), c1 = sqrt(1 - beta_t)(1 - alpha-bar_{t-1}) / (1 - alpha-bar_t), beta-tilde_t = (1 - alpha-bar_{t-1}) beta_t / (1 - alpha-bar_t), and no noise at t = 1. DDIM with K steps: times tau_i = round(1000(1 - i/K)), i = 0..K; eps-hat = (x_t - sqrt(alpha-bar_t) x-hat_0) / sqrt(1 - alpha-bar_t); x_{tau_{i+1}} = sqrt(alpha-bar_{tau_{i+1}}) x-hat_0 + sqrt(1 - alpha-bar_{tau_{i+1}}) eps-hat. Animate about 60 frames whatever K is (draw every (K/60)-th step for DDPM). Cost: 1000 steps x 1000 points x 24 components is about 2.4e7 exponentials; run in chunks with requestAnimationFrame so the page stays responsive. widgets.teaching_point: Each propagation step replaces a node's features by a degree-weighted average over its neighbourhood: after k steps a node carries information from k hops away, and after many steps every node of a connected graph points the same way (over-smoothing) at a rate set by |lambda_2|; unnormalised sums explode, and graphs that message passing cannot distinguish stay identical.
controls: slider: propagation steps k, integer 0-40, default 2
select: graph - 'cooling-system fault tree (12 nodes)' (default), 'path (12 nodes)', 'hexagon + two triangles (12 nodes)'
select: normalisation - 'symmetric D^-1/2 (A+I) D^-1/2' (default), 'random walk D^-1 (A+I)', 'none (A+I)'
click a node: pin it to the feature panel (up to three; defaults E1, E2, E7)
displays: SVG drawing of the graph at fixed coordinates; node fill = RGB from the node's 3-component feature vector after k steps, each vector divided by its own largest component so that colour shows the mix (OR red, AND blue, basic event green); node label = name
feature panel: the 3 numbers of each pinned node at step k, to 3 decimals
line chart: mean pairwise cosine similarity of node features for k = 0..40, with the current k marked
eigenvalue strip: the eigenvalues of the propagation matrix, sorted, with lambda_1 and |lambda_2| highlighted and the readout |lambda_2|^k
readout: largest absolute feature value at step k (shows the explosion under 'none')
widgets.defaults: Cooling-system fault tree, symmetric normalisation with self-loops, k = 2: the basic events under OR gates (E1, E5, E6) are already tinted red and those under AND gates (E2-E4, E7, E8) blue, and the cosine chart shows the climb toward 1 that is still to come.
widgets.spec: Graph 1, the cooling-system fault tree: nodes 0 TOP 'Loss of cooling' (OR), 1 G1 'All pumps fail' (AND), 2 G2 'Flow path blocked' (OR), 3 E1 'Power supply fails', 4 E2 'Pump A fails', 5 E3 'Pump B fails', 6 E4 'Pump C fails', 7 E5 'Valve V1 stuck closed', 8 E6 'Pipe blocked', 9 G3 'Both controllers fail' (AND), 10 E7 'Controller C1 fails', 11 E8 'Controller C2 fails'; undirected edges (0,1), (0,2), (0,3), (1,4), (1,5), (1,6), (2,7), (2,8), (2,9), (9,10), (9,11). Layout in a 680 x 360 viewBox: TOP (340, 40); G1 (130, 130), E1 (340, 130), G2 (530, 130); E2 (50, 230), E3 (130, 230), E4 (210, 230), E5 (450, 230), E6 (530, 230), G3 (610, 230); E7 (570, 320), E8 (650, 320). Features one-hot [OR, AND, basic]; gates drawn as rounded squares labelled OR/AND, basic events as circles. The single points of failure are E1, E5 and E6 (as in Lab 3). Graph 2, path: 12 nodes in a line, node 0 = (1, 0, 0), node 11 = (0, 0, 1), the others (0, 1, 0). Graph 3: two triangles (nodes 0-2 and 3-5) and a hexagon (nodes 6-11 in a ring), every feature (0.5, 0.5, 0.5). Propagation: A-tilde = A + I with self-loops, else A; d-tilde = row sums of A-tilde; symmetric P = D-tilde^-1/2 A-tilde D-tilde^-1/2; random walk P = D-tilde^-1 A-tilde; none P = A-tilde. H_0 = X, H_k = P H_{k-1}; precompute H_0..H_40 (12 x 3 each). Cosine: mean over the 66 node pairs of h_i . h_j / (|h_i| |h_j|). Eigenvalues: Jacobi rotations on the symmetric matrix (for random walk use the symmetric matrix, which has the same eigenvalues). No node has degree 0 in these graphs. Random walk: cosine 0.780 (1), 0.943 (4), 0.987 (8), 0.998 (16); the rows become identical. None: largest eigenvalue 3.392; largest feature 3 (k = 1), 26 (3), 1.05e3 (6), 1.22e4 (8), 1.2e21 (40), shown in scientific notation with the colour scale capped. Symmetric without self-loops: the tree is bipartite, the eigenvalues include -1, and the cosine oscillates 0.455, 0.384, 0.762, 0.661, 0.832 (k = 0-4), settling near 0.976 and never reaching 1. writer_notes:
GENERAL. This module is wide: seven families in thirteen sections. Depth is uneven by design: Sections 3 (VAE), 5-6 (diffusion), 7-8 (GNN) and 9 (PINN) are the deep ones; GANs, contrastive learning and MoE are shorter but still derive their one central result. Every section follows the series order: the problem, intuition, the formalism with the derivation written out, a worked example in numbers, code or the lab link, failure modes. Equations in this outline are in plain-text shorthand (alpha-bar_t, sqrt, ||.||); write them in LaTeX with the series notation (bold vectors and matrices, theta for parameters, natural logs).

NOTATION (shared by all writers). Autoencoder: encoder f_phi, decoder g_theta, data dimension d_x, code dimension d_z (do not use E and D for encoder and decoder: D is the discriminator and the degree matrix). VAE: q_phi(z|x), p_theta(x|z), prior p(z) = N(0, I); beta with no subscript is the KL weight. GAN: G, D, p_g. Diffusion: beta_t (always subscripted), alpha_t = 1 - beta_t, alpha-bar_t = prod alpha_s, T steps, t in {1..T}, eps_theta(x_t, t, c), x-hat_0; guidance scale w with w = 1 the conditional model (state once that Ho and Salimans write (1 + w)). Graphs: G = (V, E) in calligraphic letters, n nodes, A, A-tilde = A + I, D-tilde (bold), A-hat, H^(l), N(v). PINN: u_theta, residual operator N[u], condition operator B[u], weights lambda; dimensionless time is t-hat (not tau, which is the contrastive temperature). Contrastive: sim = cosine, tau temperature, N candidates per anchor, B the batch (the series fixes B for the batch: SimCLR's B inputs give 2B views, so N = 2B - 1 and collapse gives log(2B - 1); CLIP's similarity matrix is B x B). MoE: E experts (italic E, distinct from the calligraphic edge set), k active, router g, lambda_bal.

RUNNING EXAMPLES, used across sections, so keep the numbers identical. (1) The exact linear-Gaussian model p(z) = N(0, 1), p(x|z) = N(z, 1), x = 2: Section 1's KL values 1.1534 and 0.5966 are the ELBO gap and KL term of Section 3. (2) 8x8 digits: Section 2's anomaly numbers and Section 3's collapse numbers come from Lab 1. (3) Two moons (Lab 2, Sections 5-6) and the ring of 8 Gaussians (diffusion explorer, GAN schematic). (4) Fault trees: the five-node tree (Section 7's hand computation, Section 8's over-smoothing numbers), the 12-node cooling-system tree (message-passing explorer, Lab 3 step 2 and step 8, single points of failure E1, E5, E6), and the Lab 3 generator. (5) The damped oscillator w0 = 2 pi rad/s, zeta = 0.1, everywhere: Section 9's two hand examples, Lab 4, e11, and the heat-equation exercise e12 that starts from Lab 4's code. Do not switch to w0 = 2 rad/s for easier arithmetic; at t = 0.25 s the residual of cos(w0 t) is still a hand calculation (sin(pi/2) = 1, r = -0.8 pi^2 = -7.90). (6) Synthetic vibration windows (Section 11, Lab 5, Section 13); e14(c) contrasts Lab 5's arbitrary window starts with engine windows aligned to the cycle.

SESSIONS AND EXERCISES. No run of reading in the study plan exceeds about 40 minutes: e1 follows Sections 1-2, e2 follows Section 3, and e6 sits between Sections 5 and 6. Exercises test transfer, so none reuses a worked example's numbers or cases, and no check or lab extension answers an exercise: e2's KL values, e10's K_{3,3} and prism, e13's heat sink and weld images and e14's ply, micrograph and engine cases are deliberately new; Section 4's checks leave e5 to the reader, 'What goes wrong' quotes T = 200 rather than e7's T = 100, and Lab 3's last extension points to e9 instead of stating the leaf rule. Keep it that way when writing.

NUMBERS. Every number in this outline was computed: the worked examples with exact arithmetic, the lab numbers from prototype runs (Python 3.11, PyTorch 2.x CPU build, scikit-learn 1.x, a desktop CPU). Later phases execute the labs and replace expected outputs with the real ones; when they differ in the last digits, the prose that cites lab numbers (Sections 2, 3, 6, 8, 9, 11, 13 and 'What goes wrong') must be updated to match. Some lab quantities are fragile and are given as ranges: the undirected-GCN accuracies in Lab 3 move by one or two points with the thread count (L = 4 gave 0.962 on two threads and 0.944 on four); phenomena, not digits, are the contract. Say 'last digits may differ' at each expected output.

DEPARTURES FROM THE EDITOR'S SUGGESTIONS, with reasons. (a) Lab 5 is contrastive learning on synthetic vibration signals, not on digits and not a GAN. A prototype SimCLR on 8x8 digits barely beat raw pixels (linear probe 0.659 against 0.639 with one label per class), so it taught nothing; a prototype non-saturating GAN on a ring of 8 Gaussians covered all 8 modes on three seeds and WGAN-GP failed to train at lr 1e-3, so mode collapse is too setting-sensitive to promise as a lab output. GANs therefore get a schematic figure (fig-05-9, labelled as illustrative), exercises e4 and e5, quiz question 4, and an optional Lab 2 extension. Never state measured mode-collapse numbers. (b) Lab 3 uses synthetic fault trees rather than Zachary's karate club: networkx is not in the lab environment, the engineering flavour is required, and the task (single points of failure) has an instructive baseline and a clean depth story. (c) A second widget (message-passing explorer) makes over-smoothing visible. (d) Lab 4 is the damped-oscillator ODE; the source's heat-equation exercise stays as the starred-three exercise e12. (e) Diffusion takes two sections, and neural operators get their own short section. (f) Lab 2 uses a cosine schedule with T = 200 and beta capped at 0.5 (not the paper's 0.999): with the 0.999 cap the first reverse step multiplies errors by 31.6 and the w = 7 guided samples diverged in a prototype. Explain the cap in Lab 2 and in 'What goes wrong'. (g) Section 1 gathers the shared mathematical toolkit.

AUGMENTATION CLAIMS. The source's failure mode (augmentations that remove the information the task needs) is kept as a conceptual point with the 6/9 rotation and corrosion-colour examples. Do not claim that Lab 5 demonstrates it: prototype attempts (gain 0.25-4 and 0.1-10, random low-pass filtering, time-stretch 0.5-2) did not hurt the probe on h, because the classes differ in several cues; a rotation-augmented encoder on 8x8 digits did not confuse 6 and 9 either. Lab 5 demonstrates the converse (removing the needed time-shift augmentation) and reports the wide-gain result honestly as an extension.

PUBLIC-SITE RULES (BRIEF.md). The source was written inside a private codebase. Do not mention it, its file paths, its tools, its plans or its checkers. The generic replacements are in generalised_refs; the source's named finite-element package becomes 'a finite-element solver'. GSN and SysML are public notations and may be named; spell out Goal Structuring Notation at first use.

CROSS-MODULE LINKS. Module 01: maximum likelihood, cross-entropy, PCA, baselines and leakage (the split-by-tree rule). Module 02: autodiff (PINN derivatives), Adam, training loops, debugging. Module 03: weight sharing (GCN analogy), U-Net (diffusion backbone), 1D convolution. Module 04: Bahdanau attention (GAT), anomaly detection from forecasting residuals. Module 06 comes after this one: explain the transformer FFN and attention locally in one sentence where Sections 8, 11 and 12 need them, and link forward rather than assuming them. Module 07-08: next-token prediction as self-supervision; LLM-scale MoE engineering (expert parallelism, capacity at scale) is Module 08's, so Section 12 stays at the concept and counting level. Module 10: MoE memory at serving and the cost of many sampling steps. The AI Agents series (../agent/index.html) covers retrieval-augmented generation; Section 11 links it in one sentence for CLIP-style embeddings and does not cover retrieval.

FACTS AND DATES. Date landscape statements 'as of 2026' (GANs versus diffusion; MoE in current large models). Use only the model facts given here: Mixtral 8x7B's configuration and its reported 47B total / 13B active; DeepSeek-V3's 671B total / 37B active and its auxiliary-loss-free balancing; CLIP's 400 million pairs; MAE's 75% masking; Ho et al.'s T = 1000 and beta range; Nichol and Dhariwal's s = 0.008 and 0.999 clip; Switch's lambda_bal = 0.01; latent diffusion's factor-8, 4-channel latent as one configuration of Rombach et al. Refer to paper sections by name, not number. Do not quote numbers from the guided-reading papers in the module text; the reading questions ask the reader to find them.

LABS. Each lab is self-contained (run its code blocks in order in one session), fixes seeds (torch.manual_seed(0), numpy default_rng(0), seeded torch.Generator for shuffling), prints the quantities named in its steps in the order given, and saves figures with matplotlib. Lab 4 calls torch.set_num_threads(1) and says why: a network this small gains nothing from threads, and one thread avoids oversubscription slowdowns (prototype: about 1.2 ms per step either way when alone, 30 ms with four threads while other jobs ran). Lab 2 offers QUICK = True (8,000 steps); all labs run in under 5 minutes on a laptop CPU, so no lab needs the 15-minute allowance. No lab downloads anything; networkx and graph libraries are not used.

WIDGETS. Both widgets are fully specified in 'widgets', including reference values computed with a Python implementation of the same maths, which the JS developer should reproduce as tests. The diffusion explorer sits in Section 5 and is referred to again in Section 6 (step counts); the message-passing explorer sits in Section 8 and is referred to in Section 7 (the explosion without normalisation).

VOICE TRAPS. British spelling (normalisation, parameterisation, optimiser, modelling, behaviour). No hype; GAN, PINN and neural-operator claims are always paired with how they fail and what baseline to check. Do not open sections with rhetorical questions.
